Gamaliel Asis Cordoba entered President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration in 2022 when Commission on Audit (COA) chairperson Jose Calida resigned just months into his post.

On November 13, Cordoba’s strong ties with Marcos became apparent again after the President picked him as his third appointee to the Supreme Court (SC). Cordoba replaced former associate justice Amy Lazaro Javier, an appointee of former president Rodrigo Duterte, who retired on November 16.

He is the latest Marcos appointee to the High Court after Associate Justice Raul Villanueva in 2025, and recently, Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda on November 5. He is the country’s 196th SC associate justice.

This brings the number of Marcos appointees to the High Court to three, compared with two appointed by the late former president Benigno Aquino III and nine by former president Rodrigo Duterte. Zalameda’s appointment as chief justice leaves another vacancy in the associate justice post.

Cordoba served for four years and a month in COA, the government institution mandated to audit government finances and purchases. In 2022 and 2023, he was external auditor of the International Labour Organization.

Under Cordoba, COA issued a notice of disallowance on Vice President Sara Duterte’s P73-million confidential funds for the Office of the Vice President (OVP), and P75 million for the Department of Education (DepEd)
While COA has already cleared the DepEd funds, it affirmed with finality the disallowance against the OVP. (READ: With finality: COA affirms disallowance of Sara Duterte’s P73-M confidential funds)

It was also under Cordoba in 2024 when the commission started delaying the publication of its Annual Audit Reports or AAR. Budget transparency advocates, journalists, and even politicians rely on AARs to check how agencies used their funds and if there are red flags from these transactions.
Advocates criticized the delay in publication, asserting that it neither indicated transparency nor established credibility.

blocks.caption: COA delays publishing of audit reports. How can this affect us?

blocks.text: Cordoba was the longest serving commissioner of the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) — from 2009 to 2022.
He was the NTC commissioner when former president Duterte waged a campaign against media giant ABS-CBN that ultimately led to the network’s shutdown.

At the height of the controversy, Cordoba said in one of the legislative inquiries in 2020 that the NTC would “most likely” issue a provisional authority so ABS-CBN could continue operating pending a franchise renewal. Cordoba also said at the time that ABS-CBN had no standing penalties with the NTC.
But ABS-CBN’s franchise expired and was not renewed during Duterte’s term. Its shutdown led to the retrenchment of around 5,000 personnel.
When Cordoba was still with the NTC, the website of alternative news site Bulatlat was also blocked.

Before the end of Duterte’s term in 2022, then-national security adviser Hermogenes Esperon Jr. wrote to Cordoba, requesting the commission to “order Philippine Internet Service Providers (ISPs) to block access to the following websites affiliated [with] and are supporting these terrorists and terrorist organizations.”
Esperon used the highly contested anti-terror law to justify the request. He also cited affiliations with terrorist organizations without providing substantial evidence.
After a legal battle, Bulatlat’s website was unblocked after the news site won against the NTC and Esperon in court.
But this was not the only issue that Cordoba got embroiled in.

A Rappler investigation in 2024 showed that the family of Cordoba’s wife, Monica Elena Cordoba, partly owns the commercial fishing company Mercidar Fishing Corporation. A copy of Cordoba’s 2023 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth obtained by Rappler showed that he was also a shareholder of Mercidar in 2015 and 2019 — the years when he was already with the NTC.

To avoid conflicts of interest, Section 9 of the Code of Conduct for Public Officials requires officials to divest themselves of their shareholdings or financial interest within 60 days of taking office. Rappler found that during Cordoba’s time in the NTC, the commission stopped issuing service numbers for trackers that would prevent unregulated fishing.
Mercidar is central to the municipal waters issue. Originally, 15-kilometer municipal waters were exclusively for small fisherfolk.

But in December 2023, Malabon City Regional Trial Court Judge Zaldy Docena allowed Mercidar to operate within the 15-kilometer municipal waters except in shallow waters (less than 7 fathoms deep). A year later, in 2024, the SC affirmed this decision.

blocks.caption: Top officials with private interests spoil effort to track big fishers

blocks.text: Although not a politician, Cordoba has proven to be somewhat of a political survivor, having served under four presidents: Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, Aquino, Duterte, and Marcos.
Arroyo appointed him in 2009, and the succeeding presidents kept him as part of their administrations until his appointment to the COA, an independent body.

His COA profile claimed that Cordoba’s stint in the NTC saw the improvement in the country’s internet connectivity. It also said that under him, the NTC broke the long-time duopoly in the country’s telecommunications industry.

“The country’s fixed broadband and mobile internet speeds remarkably improved globally under his leadership with Ookla Speedtest Global Index now ranking the Philippines 41st out of 180 countries globally for fixed broadband and 79th out of 140 countries for mobile,” said Cordoba’s profile.

“… The NTC broke the long-time duopoly in the telecommunications industry by successfully selecting a third telco through a most transparent bidding process under the guidance of the International Telecommunication Union,” it added.
Cordoba is a government official through and through. In 2010, Arroyo gave him the Presidential Medal of Merit “for his exemplary performance and service delivery to the Filipino people.”
He has also held the following positions in government:

items: director of the Office of Presidential Chief of Staff (2001-2002)
assistant executive secretary (2002-2003)
undersecretary, Office of the President (2003-2006)
appointments secretary, Office of the President (2006-2007)
member of board of directors, Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (2008-2009)

blocks.text: Before joining government, Cordoba worked as an associate lawyer at Siguion Reyna, Montecillo and Ongsiako Law Offices. He also worked as a tax lawyer at accounting firm SyCip Gorres Velayo and Co.

The new SC associate justice joined the long list of High Court magistrates who are products of the Ateneo de Manila University. He earned his economics degree from the university in 1992, then his juris doctor four years later. Cordoba passed the Bar in 1997 with Roll No. 42213.
Like Zalameda, Cordoba is a member of the Fraternal Order of Utopia.

blocks.caption: What will Gamaliel Cordoba, Marcos’ newest SC pick, bring to Padre Faura?

blocks.text: To secure his SC appointment, Cordoba had to beat other strong contenders.

Some of the shortlisted nominees for the post have been serving in the judiciary for decades, or are respected lawyers like Solicitor General Darlene Marie Berberabe, whom Marcos did not pick in the last two selections for SC justice.
Cordoba applied only once and got the job.

blocks.caption: Who are the candidates short-listed for SC associate justice?

blocks.text: During his Judicial and Bar Council interview on October 13, Cordoba said he applied for the position because he felt like it was the “time” to seek higher office. He said he believed it was his chance to affect more people and have a lasting legacy in public service.

Given his experience with mainly executive offices, the new justice said he would bring to the SC en banc a different perspective in handling cases. He said he believed that while having judicial experience was an advantage for an associate justice, his executive experience was something that should be considered too.
“We’re bringing many facets and many fresh new ideas which we can inject into the decisions,” he said.

As an associate justice, Cordoba promised to support the SC’s Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations or SPJI. He said the program has to continue and be expanded even more, adding that the initiative brings the courts closer to people.
SPJI is the brainchild of former chief justice Alexander Gesmundo that introduced innovations in the judiciary, including digitalization. The project has been running since 2022 and will end in 2027.

blocks.caption: What will Gamaliel Cordoba, Marcos’ newest SC pick, bring to Padre Faura?

blocks.text: As an SC justice, Cordoba said he would be the type who would follow what’s written in the 1987 Constitution and existing jurisprudence. He said he would act according to the Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability.
Cordoba also said he would inhibit himself if cases he participated in under the NTC, COA, and related offices found their way to the Supreme Court. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea ‘no longer usable’ after Kyiv strike | First Thing
articles.summary:
Blow to Kremlin as prestigious bridge linking occupied Ukrainian peninsula struck by missile. Plus, what is in store for Robert Pattinson, the new 007?

Good morning.

blocks.text: Good morning. Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section.

Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it. The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait.
Hundreds arrested at anti-Trump protests in the Philippines

blocks.caption: Demonstrators hold signs during a protest in Manila. Photograph: Firdia Linsawati/AP

blocks.text: Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as authorities braced for more protests before the US president’s arrival. Organisers say they expect as many as 10,000 people to join protests against Trump as he attends the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people, with large parts of the Philippine capital closed off and tight security in place. Some protesters burned effigies of the US president, and demonstrators angry at the cost-of-living and energy shock caused by the Iran war tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center, but were blocked by police.

items: You can follow developments at the Apec and Asean summits with our live blog.

blocks.text: Third US aircraft carrier brings thousands more troops to Middle East

blocks.caption: US Navy handout shows USS Theodore Roosevelt alongside the Royal Australian HMAS Stalwart. Photograph: US NAVY/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central Command has said, making a dramatic show of military might as Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war. USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East. Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than eight-month-old war “militarily is effectively over”.
The Roosevelt joins the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.
Microsoft identifies months-old bug as a root cause of global outage

blocks.caption: Microsoft signage at an office building in New York. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other software last week. An initial report identified three factors: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own but, taken together, led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives said.
Cornell announces full review of Greek life after scrutiny over sexual assault case

blocks.caption: Hundreds of Cornell students participate in a rally against the university. Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty Images

blocks.text: Cornell University is to announce a “full review” of fraternities and sororities determining their future on campus, after an alleged sexual assault brought scrutiny to the system at the Ivy League school. The university’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced the review in an update outlining several steps the institution had taken after a woman said she was gang-raped at an on-campus fraternity’s house. Cornell had already banned fraternity parties for the rest of the academic year.
In other news …

blocks.caption: The US women’s ice hockey team celebrate. Photograph: Ida Marie Odgaard/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP/Getty Images

items: The US has beaten Canada to win the women’s ice hockey world championship in Denmark, becoming the first US team to capture Olympic and world titles in the same calendar year.
A judge has scheduled Lindsay Clancy’s second trial in the killings of her three young children for late March, over the objections of prosecutors.
Dolores Huerta has been honored in a ceremony at California’s state capitol.
Authorities investigating a bomb found at an ethanol production plant in Illinois have taken a suspect into custody, according to the mayor there.
California is suing OpenAI, accusing the artificial intelligence company of developing its technology without safety or the public’s interest in mind.
Several companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump’s tariffs have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, an investigation has found.
Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, has announced he is disbanding a city police unit accused of using excessive force.

blocks.text: Stat of the day: Freeman Johnson, oldest survivor of Pearl Harbor attack, dies aged 106

blocks.caption: Freeman Johnson. Photograph: Charles Krupa/AP

blocks.text: The oldest known survivor of the Pearl Harbor attack has died aged 106. Freeman Johnson, a firefighter below the deck during the attack, told the Associated Press in May: “While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing.” Only 11 known Pearl Harbor survivors are still living, all of whom are centenarians.
Culture Pick: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond – so what happens next?

blocks.caption: Robert Pattinson. Photograph: Jaap Buitendijk/Amazon MGM Studios/AP

blocks.text: Andrew Pulver writes that the wait for the new Bond is over, but that’s only the beginning – there are still small issues such as the script, title, setting, casting, branding and promotion of the next instalment of the franchise. Nadia Khomami, meanwhile, traces Pattinson’s journey from Harry Potter and Twilight to 007.
Don’t miss this: ‘His wife was horrified’ – did Edward Hopper paint his sexual problems?

blocks.caption: A visitor views an art exhibition of works by American painter Edward Hopper. Photograph: Michele Tantussi/Getty Images

blocks.text: In a new biography, the maestro of American melancholy is called a “sadist” and a “prize hog” by his wife – who was aghast to see their domestic and bedroom problems surface in his most famous works. Louis Shadwick explains.
… or this: ‘Nothing they said made sense’ – down the rabbit hole with sovereign citizens

blocks.caption: Illustration: Guardian Design / Anaïs Mims/Getty

blocks.text: Described by Mark Blacklock as “the perfect conspiracy model for consumer capitalist societies”, this is a fascinating read about how a convicted fraudster from North Dakota and a white supremacist inspired the “sovereign citizen” movement. It has blossomed around the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives along the way.
Climate check: Surge of US datacenters adds equivalent of Denmark’s annual emissions

blocks.caption: An Amazon datacenter under construction. Photograph: Jeff Roberson/AP

blocks.text: The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler” datacenters in the US has collectively caused planet-heating emissions of about the same scale as Denmark emits in a year, research has found. Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia, meanwhile, have been named as the biggest CO2 exporters in history in a new analysis of data since 1850.

items: Follow the latest from Cop31 with Ajit Niranjan on our live blog.

blocks.text: Last Thing: Band of baby sea turtles swims into ocean after historic California nesting

blocks.caption: An olive ridley sea turtle hatchling. Photograph: Johan Ordóñez/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific. Hopefully they will thrive better than Fiona the hippo is doing at the moment – she is under veterinary care after eating a hat at Cincinnati zoo.

articles.title: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
articles.summary:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy

In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of…

blocks.text: In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow.

On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.

The broader Apec summit, meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.

blocks.caption: A humanoid robot serves a cup of coffee at the Apec media centre in Shenzhen. Photograph: Tingshu Wang/Reuters

blocks.text: All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.

“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”

blocks.caption: A light show in Shenzhen on Sunday. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images

blocks.text: Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.

Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.

blocks.caption: Mark Carney and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday. Photograph: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/AP

blocks.text: A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.

The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”

blocks.caption: Xi and Donald Trump at the White House in September. Photograph: Abaca/Shutterstock

blocks.text: China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”

The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.

The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”

blocks.caption: Nesting dolls depicting Xi, Trump and Vladimir Putin in a gift shop in Moscow. Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”

For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

articles.title: Nvidia partner Megaspeed being investigated by US government over chip exports
articles.summary: The Singapore-based company is suspected of helping to ship high-end AI chips from tech giant Nvidia to China, violating US export rules.

blocks.text: The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.

Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.

items: Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China

blocks.text: In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".

They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

articles.title: Ikea ditches plans for new UK stores, blaming high business taxes
articles.summary: Retailer’s British boss says John Healey ‘missed opportunity to back retailers’ in October’s budget

blocks.text: Ikea has ditched some planned store openings in the UK blaming the cost of business taxes, which it said were the highest in Europe.

As its annual UK sales little more than flatlined at the Swedish flatpack furniture retailer, its UK boss, David McCabe, said: “There are locations where we were planning to open a new unit, and those plans have been abandoned due to the cost that we experience and the complexity within the market.
“I would hope that we’re able to bring those projects back to life,” he added. “But it’s a very real impact here in the UK, when those investments will go to other countries in Europe.”

The planned investments were smaller UK stores, but the retailer declined to comment on exact locations. Ikea has been pushing further into smaller high street shops, rather than its traditional out-of-town outlets.
Ikea’s UK arm pays the most business taxes of its operations in Europe, and the third highest in the world, after the US and China, he said.

The retailer’s UK sales edged 0.5% higher to £2.26bn in the year to the end of August. Sales rose 4.7% in the first four months of the year but fell in the second half as weak confidence and “sustained pressure” on household budgets led consumers to pull back on big purchases.

McCabe said he had talked to customers in stores in recent weeks who were planning to replace an entire bedroom, but then decided to just buy one or two smaller pieces of furniture and a refresh with new textiles to save money.

“We are seeing a change in the way that customers shop and we do anticipate a difficult period going forward,” he said. “We don’t think that there’s going to be a sudden, miraculous turnaround in confidence.”
McCabe described John Healey’s recent budget as a “missed opportunity to back retailers under real pressure”, but said Ikea continued to talk to the government.
The company has spent £54m on reducing prices by an average of 20% on 425 products, including its popular Billy bookcase, Hemnes daybed and the cantilever Poäng armchair.
after newsletter promotion
Ikea is using seasonal offers to pull in customers, for example discounts on extendable dining tables, folding chairs and soft toys in the run-up to Christmas.
McCabe said smaller stores, between 1,000 and 2,000 sq metres, had been popular with customers, in sites such as Oxford Street in London and retail parks.

As well as the Oxford Street shop which opened within the former Topshop flagship site, Ikea opened stores in Brighton, Norwich and York last year, followed by a small store in Chester. It also opened a “plan and order” site – dedicated to kitchen, bedroom, and living room planning – in Dundee, and one in Aberdeen last month.

articles.title: UK music industry hits record high of £8.4bn – but are working musicians being left behind?
articles.summary:
Major tours by the likes of Oasis helped make 2025 a lucrative year, with music export revenue reaching £4.8bn

Major tours by Oasis, Robbie Williams and Dua Lipa, as well as hit albums by…

blocks.text: Major tours by Oasis, Robbie Williams and Dua Lipa, as well as hit albums by the likes of Olivia Dean, have helped to push the UK music industry to record revenues.
But there are concerns over a widening gulf in income between A-listers such as these, and the less well-known artists that form the bulk of the UK’s music community.

The annual report by UK Music, an umbrella organisation featuring various industry bodies, finds that music added £8.4bn to the UK economy in 2025, a record figure and an inflation-outpacing rise of 5.7% from the previous year.

Export revenue rose 3.6%, to £4.8bn, encompassing money made outside the UK by British artists – including via international touring and royalties and revenues raised from sales and streaming of music abroad.
There was also a slight rise in employment in the sector in the UK: 730 jobs were added, to take total recorded employment to 220,500.

The success is powered in part by a live music sector in which stadium performances – once the preserve of only the very top artists – are becoming increasingly commonplace, with consumers willing to spend three-figure sums on tickets.

However, the This Is Music report cautioned that “many emerging and grassroots artists experienced rising costs which reduced net incomes, and even well-known artists have found it hard to make money”.

The report highlights a number of hit albums by UK artists that have helped boost recorded music revenues – including No 1s by Sleep Token, Yungblud, Sam Fender, Wet Leg, and Biffy Clyro – but also highlighted a troubling trend.

blocks.caption: British metal band Sleep Token, who scored a No 1 album in 2025. Photograph: Helle Arensbak/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In terms of album consumption figures, UK artists had historically been more popular than US ones in the domestic marketplace, but US artists overtook UK ones in 2018 and their popularity has continued to diverge, levelling out somewhat in 2025 thanks in part to blockbuster hits by Dean, Fender and others.

AI also threatens to divert listeners’ attention away from human artists, with the report warning: “AI generated ‘slop’ and deepfakes are an increasing problem, which is reflected in a dramatic increase in takedown notices for AI deepfakes issued by labels,” referring to songs taken down from streaming services for imitating existing artists.

There was a marked difference between two sets of data the study used to monitor the income of artists. A survey of the accounts for “top and mid-level” artists found that these musicians were flush, their earnings rising more than 14% year on year. But the Music Creators’ Survey, which asks musicians (including artists, songwriters, producers, composers and more) to self-report their income, found growth of just 0.2% in the same period.

“It has never been easier to record and release music, but given the intense level of competition that has ensued, it has never been more difficult to establish a profile and build a scalable career,” reads the report. “This makes life especially tough for many music creators with average earnings.

“Once artists and music creators break through beyond a certain level, more options and better terms of business can enhance their careers very significantly, but the challenge remains developing more artists and creators to that level.”

UK Music is made up of industry bodies, including royalty agencies PRS for Music and PPL; the BPI, the collective body for the UK’s record labels; AIM, which represents the independent label sector; plus the Musicians’ Union and more.

Tom Kiehl, UK Music’s chief executive, used the report’s launch to lobby the government on a range of issues. “The government must use the upcoming UK EU summit on 20 November to work to remove barriers to EU exports,” he said. “It must not give AI a free pass and should support a sustainably funded BBC – and deliver economic growth for music in every postcode.

He added: “We are not simply asking government to act. We stand ready to be part of the solution too. The UK music industry has never lacked talent, ambition or creativity. The challenge now is ensuring the right environment exists for those strengths to flourish. If we get that right, the opportunities ahead are enormous.”

Ian Murray, creative industries minister, highlighted government funding schemes such as the Music Growth Package and said: “We are investing in the grassroots infrastructure, talent pipeline and independent businesses that keep the sector competitive.”
Some of the UK’s most successful acts are already eyeing a potentially lucrative 2027.

Oasis will head back out on tour after the blockbuster success of their 2025 reunion, playing 11 different locations across the UK, Europe and North America; Dua Lipa has been announced as a headliner of Coachella festival and is expected to release a fourth studio album; and Sam Fender has announced the Proper Massive tour, with 12 UK and Ireland stadium dates plus major venues in North America.

articles.title: What do Democrats’ sweeping midterm wins mean for Trump’s ICE crackdown?
articles.summary:
Despite House and Senate majorities, Democrats face a battle to enact legislation – but they have the power to conduct tough new oversight

The Democrats’

blocks.text: The Democrats’ midterm “blue wave” wins gave them strong majorities in both chambers of Congress, new governors’ mansions and power in some unexpected places. Voters dealt a stunning rebuke to Donald Trump – and his ruthless deportation campaign and violent ICE raids across the country were among the key issues that cost Republicans support. But what will Democrats do about the immigration crackdown?
Can congressional Democrats rein in ICE?

blocks.caption: Observers film ICE agents in Minneapolis in February. Photograph: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images

blocks.text: The US Congress theoretically has the ability to force many changes on ICE through legislation, such as taking away funds, restricting detention centers and mandating a focus on migrants with violent records – after Trump’s pledges to target “the worst of the worst” actually turned into mass arrests of people without criminal records and even of people with legal papers.

Democrats have said such things as, “We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities [have] killed individuals … assaulted individuals… incarcerated individuals” (Mississippi Representative Bennie Thompson, likely to chair the House homeland security committee), and “We will rip ICE apart” (incoming US Senator of Minnesota Peggy Flanagan).

But even with House and Senate majorities, enacting legislation will face steep odds without Republicans on board, considering presidential veto power and the Senate filibuster, which requires at least 60 votes to move bills forward.
And not everyone in the Democratic caucus is on the same page. Leaders are initially proposing more modest guardrails, banning masks for ICE officers and requiring body-worn cameras in the field.

In practice, one of the clearest unilateral powers Democrats will have next year is that of greater oversight, conducting investigations to expose the faults of the Trump administration’s immigration policy.
What could oversight look like?

blocks.caption: A federal agent sprays a chemical agent at protesters outside Delaney Hall in Newark in May. Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian

blocks.text: Democratic-led congressional committees will be able to issue subpoenas, and they already plan to call in homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin, new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, border czar Tom Homan and former border patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino for questioning in public.

They may also hold hearings in cities where they can present evidence of agency misconduct, while continuing congressional visits to ICE detention facilities to check on conditions there and increase public exposure.

Meanwhile, they could consider impeachment. It is unclear whether the US constitution allows for someone like Miller, as chief of staff, to be impeached. But if Democrats lead a second attempt to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth – and especially if they succeed in removing him from office – it could curtail Miller’s authority by putting other impeachable officials directing immigration enforcement, such as Mullin, on notice that they could lose their jobs if they follow any White House advice to act lawlessly.
What new laws or reforms could Democrats realistically pass?

blocks.caption: Protestors gather outside the supreme court in April as the Trump administration aims to end TPS status for Syrians and Haitians. Photograph: Jack Gruber/USA Today Network/Reuters Connect

blocks.text: Democrats, both sitting and incoming, are now pushing for comprehensive immigration changes to a system that both parties have long agreed is “broken”, but Congress has not had the will to reform top to tail, balancing security measures at the US-Mexico border with helping immigrants already in the US.

Sufficient bipartisan unity is hard to come by. Republicans largely oppose what they call “amnesty” – giving people in the country unlawfully the chance to legalize their status. Some progressive Democrats, meanwhile, denounce crackdowns on the border and restrictions on seeking asylum that contradict international law.

Yet more targeted fixes may be on the table. Some 81% of Americans endorse a citizenship pathway for undocumented immigrants who came to the US as children, also known as “Dreamers”, according to a recent Gallup poll. Even the Trump administration has indicated renewed openness to this idea since the midterm drubbing.

Lawmakers may be able to get agreement to reinstate temporary protected status (TPS), a program allowing work permits and protection from deportation for nationalities in the US who are unable to safely return to their home countries, especially for Haitians and Afghans. The administration has ended TPS for roughly a million people across more than a dozen nationalities.
Legislation could even create a pathway to a green card for TPS holders, something that does not exist now.
However, once again, with Trump threatening to become “Mr Veto” it’s unclear how he and Senate Republicans will proceed.
What about the high levels of DHS funding?

blocks.caption: US homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

blocks.text: DHS, which oversees immigration enforcement and many immigration benefits in the US, has received about a quarter of a trillion dollars in funding during Trump’s second term alone. Taxpayers’ money designated for ICE soared and it is now the highest federally-funded US law enforcement agency.

That includes a roughly $70bn cash infusion in June, meant to bankroll the department through the end of Trump’s presidency. Democrats say they plan to make efforts to claw back or withhold at least some of that funding through legislation once they control Congress.
Some Democrats want to abolish ICE – how likely is that to happen?

blocks.caption: An ‘Abolish Ice’ flag in Minnesota. Photograph: Tim Evans/Reuters

blocks.text: Very unlikely. The slogan “abolish ICE” became a political liability for Democrats as Americans turned on undocumented immigrants when unauthorized border crossings rose sharply under the Biden administration and Trump and his Maga white nationalist ranks started calling them an “invasion”. Even to many mainstream US voters the notion that you should entirely abolish ICE – like defunding the police – stood for the left being too soft on law and order.

Despite the backlash that Republicans are now feeling given the perceived cruelty of Trump’s mass deportation campaign and ICE violence on the streets, an ideological divide among progressive and more moderate Democrats would probably preclude closing down the agency.
The re-elected centrist Democratic congressman Henry Cuellar, representing a Texas-Mexico border district, last Wednesday said simply: “I’m not going to abolish ICE.”
What about the Democrats who won big at state and local level?

blocks.caption: Campaign signs for James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa in Mission, Texas. Photograph: Adam Gray/Getty Images

blocks.text: Although immigration enforcement is broadly a federal responsibility, state and local governments have been deeply involved in recent years – especially through cooperation between police and sheriffs’ departments and ICE, whether because of what’s called 287(g) agreements or other collaborative policies.
Texas, in particular, saw a political earthquake, where Democrats flipped a US Senate seat, the governorship, the attorney general’s office and the state House of Representatives.

This followed decades of Republican dominance statewide and increasingly draconian immigration enforcement. Texas’s laws and policies have required local law enforcement to work with ICE and state penalties have criminalized people who unlawfully crossed the border with Mexico.

Leadership in states that swung heavily blue now have the opportunity to back off such aggressive tactics, likely leading to fewer ICE arrests, less depletion of immigrant-heavy workforces, and the potential for communities to rebuild trust with local law enforcement.

Democrats are now set to hold all 10 of the House seats along the almost 3,000 miles of the US-Mexico border and the four border governorships – California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas – for the first time since 1979, as well as four states’ top legal offices. Hard-right Texas governor Greg Abbott, for example, outgoing after 12 years, unilaterally bussed migrants to Democratic-led cities and spent an estimated $11bn militarizing the Tex-Mex border with the extreme project, “Operation Lone Star”. Now Democrats will examine what they can and wish to unwind.
How else could Democratic state and local officials respond?

blocks.caption: Detained immigration activists stand in line to be loaded into a police bus outside the Jacob K Javits federal building in New York in September last year. Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian

blocks.text: Democratic state leaders could help reinstate policies that help immigrants, such as access to in-state college tuition for undocumented students, after those were gutted in some states amid federal collusion in Trump’s second term.

They could also join lawsuits challenging Trump-era policies, and cities, counties and states that are suddenly on the same side of the political debate could pool resources to fight legal battles against the federal government instead of against each other.

The label “sanctuary city” has somewhat gone out of vogue in recent years. But in a similar vein, Democratic city and county leaders, as well as state legislatures, may devise new laws and strategies to block cooperation with ICE, at least when it comes to immigrants who do not pose a public safety risk.
What other changes are we most likely to see?

blocks.caption: Talarico campaigns in Laredo, Texas. Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty Images

blocks.text: For federal congressional seats that have flipped in favor of Democrats, immigrants may discover a new ally. Congressional offices often help their constituents – including noncitizens – contact federal agencies, get answers from the government and sometimes find solutions. That can mean finally receiving a work permit stuck in limbo, helping a family member overseas with their visa processing or getting a loved one out of detention.
Ultimately, the president and his subordinates have given no signs that policies will be easing - and they plan to continue deportations.

Despite Trump telling 60 Minutes after the midterm losses that maybe immigration enforcement was “too tough”, he appointed the ferociously anti-immigration zealot and longtime ally Miller as his chief of staff shortly after that interview was recorded.

While Democrats can shine a spotlight on excesses and racist attitudes and act as a buffer, more transformational change will probably have to wait to see if a Democrat – particularly a progressive – wins the White House in 2028.

articles.title: New Orleans police arrest teen over beating death of homeless man ‘unable to defend himself’
articles.summary:
Police say David Hyde, 68, left with shoe prints in face from kicks to head and prescription medication stolen in attack

A man who was unhoused and “unable to defend himself due to health…
articles.byline: Ramon Antonio Vargas in New Orleans

blocks.text: A man who was unhoused and “unable to defend himself due to health issues” was recently beaten to death and had his prescription medication taken outside a pharmacy in New Orleans, according to authorities.

The killing of 68-year-old David Hyde led police to arrest Antonio Myles, 19, on a count of second-degree murder, with investigators alleging that they came to suspect the much younger man after he had bragged to others about fatally beating an unhoused person.

As portrayed in criminal court records summarizing the circumstances surrounding Myles’ arrest, Hyde’s killing is an extreme example of how people experiencing homelessness in the US are at heightened risk of being victimized by violence.

A 2020 US justice department study determined that about half of people experiencing homelessness report being victims of violence – a rate that for the general population is 2%. And in May, amid an affordability crisis in the US, the federal Housing and Urban Development said the most recent available point-in-time estimate calculated that nearly 700,000 people were experiencing homelessness nationwide when the count was conducted on a night in January.

New Orleans police said officers found Hyde down outside a Walgreens in the 4400 block of Claiborne Avenue, on the edge of the city’s Freret neighborhood, at about 6.55am on 8 November “with severe contusions to his face”. He was near numerous prescription medication bottles and pronounced dead at the scene from what investigators ascertained to be kicks to the head, as evident from the shoe prints left on Hyde’s face, police wrote in sworn count documents.

Investigators later secured video from a store surveillance camera that showed Hyde sitting near the pharmacy’s front entrance when his attacker took his backpack, dumped its contents on the ground and picked some of those items up prior to the beating. While the deadly violence evidently happened out of the camera’s view, the man who approached Hyde at one point used his shirt to wipe his shoes and then left the scene.

Police alleged they received a call a day later reporting that Myles had been heard “bragging to unknown subjects that he was responsible for beating a homeless man to death”. Myles was soon interviewed by police, but they released him pending further investigation, according to the sworn statement summarizing the case.

Then, on 10 November, police investigating Hyde’s killing released video from a surveillance camera overlooking a parking lot which depicted a figure described as a “suspect wanted in connection with a brutal beating that left a disabled man dead”.
“The victim … was unable to defend himself due to health issues,” police said in a statement accompanying the video, without elaborating. Police asked anyone who recognized the figure to call them.

An unidentified “known subject” then told police the person in the video was Myles. That person also reportedly alleged Myles was wearing a beanie-style cap at the time of Hyde’s beating. Investigators said they later recovered surveillance footage which established Myles was wearing a beanie-style cap when Hyde was killed.

Furthermore, police said that a detective interviewed an unidentified but known subject who reported that Myles had called hours after Hyde was discovered dead. The sworn police statement accused Myles of telling that person “he loved them, and that he killed a homeless man, and continued to kick him after he was already dead”.

“The known subject also advised … that Mr Myles advised a known subject that he killed the homeless man and took his prescription medication that was inside his backpack,” the sworn police statement said. Police also said that person knew Myles well and identified him as being on the video released to the public.
According to the police statement, investigators believed that information was true because “no specific details of the investigation were released to the media”.

“Only a person who was there when the homicide occurred would know that the victim was kicked to his head repeatedly, and that the victim was in possession of prescription medicine inside of a backpack,” said the police statement, which was not available to the news media until Monday.

A New Orleans criminal court magistrate commissioner gave police permission to arrest Myles on a count of murder on Friday. He soon turned himself over to police and was jailed – and no bond was immediately set for him, court records show.

Myles’ arrest in Hyde’s killing came after he pleaded guilty to a charge of simple battery on 11 August in an unrelated case and was sentenced to about a month in jail, according to court records. He would receive mandatory life imprisonment if eventually convicted of second-degree murder.

articles.title: US challenges Airbus €3 billion EIB financing, raising fears of renewed transatlantic trade tensions
articles.summary: The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.

image.caption: While the European Investment Bank has authorized up to €3 billion for Airbus, only an initial €1 billion tranche has actually been committed so farImage: Boris Roessler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business."

He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.
An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments."
A thorn in the side of EU-US trade relations
Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.
The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

She says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side" it has the potential to spiral but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.
Does the €3 billion Airbus loan amount to state support?
At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors."

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.
A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past."
Germany launches €35-billion military space program

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Centre for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establishthe full facts.

Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.
"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen."

blocks.caption: Besides commercial aviation, Airbus also contributes to defense, such as the Eurofighter program. The EU insists the new loan is above boardImage: Joan Valls/Urbanandsport/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things."
He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously."

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants.
Why Lufthansa is retiring an unusual aviation icon
Why the Airbus-Boeing subsidy dispute keeps resurfacing

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce."
She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union."

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.
"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development."

articles.title: Japan proposes creation of ‘Asian’ IEA
articles.summary: Under the initiative, Japan would also offer its unused oil storage facilities to other countries and help them develop own stockpiling systems

blocks.text: WOMAN PM. Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae arrives at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and Related Summits in Manila on November 16, 2026.
Jam Sta Rosa/Pool via Reuters
Under the initiative, Japan would also offer its unused oil storage facilities to other countries and help them develop own stockpiling systems

items: Japan proposed the creation of an Asia Oil Security Task Force to enhance cooperation on oil stockpiling and emergency supply coordination during the AZEC Leaders' Meeting in Manila.
The initiative aims to utilize Japan's unused oil storage facilities to help other countries develop their own stockpiling systems, addressing vulnerabilities exposed by the Middle East oil crisis.

The Philippines and Japan signed a memorandum of cooperation to advance the Philippines' strategic petroleum reserve, focusing on developing storage facilities and enhancing preparedness against global oil supply disruptions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Japan on Tuesday, November 17, proposed the creation of a regional task force to strengthen cooperation on oil stockpiling and coordinate the release of supplies during emergencies.
Japan Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae announced the proposed Asia Oil Security Task Force during the fourth Asia Zero-Emission Community (AZEC) Leaders’ Meeting in Manila.
“We intend to promote as an equivalent of Asian version of the IEA (International Energy Agency),” Takaichi said.

The Middle East oil crisis exposed vulnerabilities in the global and Philippine energy security, driven by heavy reliance on fossil fuels and imports and critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz.

In a separate interview, Japan Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) Press Secretary Toshihiro Kitamura elaborated on the proposal, saying that Japan — under the initiative — would offer its unused oil storage facilities to other countries and help them develop their own oil stockpiling systems.

“We have suggested to utilize our crude oil stockpiling facilities in Japan, which is not utilized. By utilizing those unused stockpiling facilities, we can stockpile in advance the crude oil purchased in Middle East or other countries,” Kitamura told reporters. (Watch this video below on how Japan’s national petroleum stockpiling helps ensure its energy security:

blocks.caption: Japan proposes creation of ‘Asian’ IEA

blocks.text: Kitamura said discussions on the proposed task force’s operational rules were still ongoing, including the possible fees other countries would pay to use Japan’s unused storage facilities.

“Under AZEC 2.0 POWERR Asia initiative, we are going to support Asian countries, especially ASEAN countries, to be more resilient by providing such a stockpiling system either individually, or jointly in the region,” he added.

Speaking at the AZEC summit, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said stockpiling alone would not be enough to ensure energy security. He said the Philippines is actively advancing its strategic petroleum reserve and welcoming “high-impact investments across our energy landscape, from renewables, grid modernization, and energy storage to natural gas, energy efficiency, and emerging technologies that contribute to overall regional energy security”.

“Sustainable and enduring energy security demands that oil-consuming and oil-producing nations act in unison. We must deepen information sharing and practical storage arrangements, as well as commit to upholding international law to keep sea lanes open and maintain fair, transparent markets,” Marcos said.
Apart from Japan and the Philippines, other AZEC partner countries include Australia, Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.

In a related development, the Philippines and Japan signed a memorandum of cooperation (MOC) to advance the country’s strategic petroleum reserve and strengthen its preparedness against global oil supply disruptions.

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin and Japan’s Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Ryosei Akazawa signed the agreement on Monday, November 16, which provides a framework for developing, managing, and releasing strategic reserves, while opening the door for Japanese participation in stockpiling projects led by the Philippine National Oil Company (PNOC).
“Japan will help us establish more storage facilities for fuel products, whether that is diesel, gas or crude oil,” Garin said.

The agreement also covers the development of oil storage facilities and the identification of financing arrangements. Japanese agencies will assist the Philippines through capacity-building, oil security assessments, and policy development, providing technical expertise and support in managing strategic reserves, Garin added.
“We can establish our own oil tanks, or ports and jetties. We do have our own storage facilities for oil. But we need to know how to manage all these strategic reserves,” she said.
“We will start on capacity-building, especially with PNOC,” Garin added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank
articles.summary:
Move is designed to hinder building of more illegal settlements, which Foreign Office says Israel has ‘refused to clamp down on’

Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against…

blocks.text: Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution.
The UK foreign secretary also announced he was placing sanctions on a rightwing activist Israeli group involved in trying to block aid into Gaza as recently as last month.

Miliband announced the measures just before tenders for the large E1 West Bank settlement were due to be allocated by the Israeli government, while saying he wanted to work with a new Israeli government in a more cooperative way.
Israel’s possible new prime minister, Gadi Eisenkot has said that, if appointed, he will take a tougher approach than Benjamin Netanyahu to settler violence.

blocks.caption: Eisenkot (left) and Netanyahu at the Knesset on 10 November. Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty Images

blocks.text: The sanctions are designed to stop the flow of finance to eight identified construction firms, although in practice the extent to which any of the firms are dependent on British finance is yet to be tested.

On 8 September, Miliband announced an expansion of its Global Human Rights sanctions regime, as well as a complex set of measures, yet to be implemented, designed to ban the trade in goods from illegal settlements. The Foreign Office said that it welcomed and encouraged trade with “green line Israel” and firmly distinguished this with activity in settlements.

The Foreign Office said the current Israeli government had “not only refused to clamp down on illegal settlement, but has facilitated and encouraged them”. More settlements had been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years.

The entities targeted by sanctions are Israeli construction, property development and architectural businesses that have helped to plan, build, supply or market housing and public infrastructure in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband – who was criticised by some for broadening the sanctions criteria and planning a ban on trade with illegal settlement – said: “Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach.

“That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution. And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza. The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.”

blocks.caption: Palestinian children at a makeshift school established inside tents in Gaza City. Photograph: Omar Ashtawy/HL/Getty Images

blocks.text: But he added in a potential olive branch: “We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike.”

Miliband and his Middle East minister, Stephen Doughty, have repeatedly highlighted the Israeli government’s refusal to let a variety of dual-use goods into Gaza. The Foreign Office said civilians in Gaza were in desperate need of winter supplies, with catastrophic floods leaving nearly 4,000 households without shelter and 1.4 million people living in tents or makeshift shelters.

According to the UN, more than 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins bought by humanitarian partners and donors are outside Gaza ready to go in, but are being held by the Israeli authorities. The Israeli authorities also continue to block timber from entering, leaving no emergency shelter kits available in Gaza.

The Israeli government claims the blockage of some goods is necessary to prevent Hamas obtaining goods that could be used to attack Israel. The dispute over dual-use goods and closed entry points into Gaza has lasted for more than two years.

articles.title: Turkish authorities raid opposition Sozcu news channel, appoint new management
articles.summary: Turkish authorities have raided the Istanbul offices of Sozcu TV, halting broadcasts, appointing a trustee and opening an investigation. This marks another crackdown on pro-opposition television…

image.caption: Sozcu TV was one of the last critical news channels in TurkeyImage: Berk Ozkan/AFP

blocks.text: Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of the pro-opposition Sozcu TV early on Tuesday, arresting admins and installing a government trustee as the head, the group said on X.
The channel announced in a predawn post that police were searching the building under a court order.
What did Sozcu say about the raid by Turkish police?
"Police are searching the Sozcu building under a court order. Police have cordoned off the building," its official X account said in just before 5 a.m. (0200 GMT).
"A trustee has been appointed to Sozcu! Police are searching the building... There have been detentions," it said, with its journalists saying staff were not being allowed inside.
According to the media group, the trustee took control of the television channel and the news website but not the print newspaper.

blocks.caption: Police officers were seen inside the headquarters Image: Berk Ozkan/AFP

blocks.text: After the raid, regular news broadcasts were stopped and a documentary was shown instead.

At noon, the channel resumed its regular coverage, mentioning the raids only at the beginning of the broadcast. One of the channel's news presenters, Damla Dogan Tuncel, said on X that the channel had challenged the decision and was awaiting a court ruling.
"In the meantime, the broadcast would continue with normal news bulletins," she said.
'Terrorism' charges
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said the action against Sozcu TV was part of an investigation into alleged breaches of Turkey's "anti-terror financing laws."

The prosecutor's office claimed that the channel had suspected links to a network that was led by US-based cleric Fethullah Gulen. The cleric, who died in 2024, was accused by Turkey of orchestrating a failed military coup in 2016.

blocks.caption: The channel continues broadcasting amid uncertainty over its futureImage: Berk Ozkan/AFP

blocks.text: Sozcu Media Group lawyer Ersan Barkin said the raids stemmed from a 2016 case that Turkey's Supreme Court had previously dismissed, finding no evidence of criminal intent or wrongdoing.
"This trustee decision stems from a file in which no offence was established," he told KRT TV.
Government silences last critical news channels
The move is the latest suppression of critical linear media in Turkey, coming a month after the police raided the country's most-watched news channel, Halk TV, and installed an administrator.
Since then, news broadcasts on the channel have remained on pause.
Another pro-opposition news channel TELE1 was also raided and seized by the government, while its owner Merdan Yanardag was jailed on espionage charges.
Over the last decade, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government has seized control of most of the media landscape, particularly television broadcasters.
While the critical voices were pushed onto the online space, Halk TV and Sozcu TV were prominent pro-opposition voices in TV.
No future in Turkey? Growing exodus of young Turks
Press freedom has suffered dramatically during Erdogan's 22 years in power.In the most recent Reporters Without Borders world press freedom index, Turkey ranked 163 of 180 countries.
Deutsche Welle correspondent Alican Uludag was also jailed and released this year on charges including insulting President Erdogan.
Opposition lashes out at the government
Opposition leader Ozgur Ozel, whose party was also raided and seized by a trustee, said "the government no longer has any tolerance left for even the slightest criticism."
"May our hearts wither if we surrender to these would-be dictators," he said on X.
Istanbul Mayor and Erdogan's jailed rival Ekrem Imamoglu said "the government's election fear is growing and growing."
"With courage, perseverance, and determination, people will continue the struggle," he said, from his blocked X account.
Turkey's Ozel launches new party to challenge Erdogan
