articles.title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.summary: The new rules restrict chip exports and also access to their computing power, which China relies on heavily.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May
ByOsmond Chia
Business reporter
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
A blow to Asia's AI boom

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

blocks.text: Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Singapore, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms. Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
A headache for China
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.

Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.

That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

blocks.text: What you need to know

Germany expects to see the highest number of new businesses opening in 2026 in more than a decade
Chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finnish President Alexander Stubb for talks expected to focus on security policy and Russia's invasion of Ukraine
A massive leak of internal documents from Deutsche Bank has exposed misconduct and incompetence at the lender, media say

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:
November 17, 2026
Rwanda migrant deportation hub scheme condemned by rights groups
A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.
The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.
The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."
Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.
"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.
"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."
In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.
"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.
"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.
Criticism from within the coalition

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).
"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.
"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.
"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."
Rwanda deportation hub planned for 2027
The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.
According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.
Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

articles.title: What makes 'Grand Theft Auto VI' more than just a game?
articles.summary: When "GTA VI" is released on November 19, millions of people worldwide will rush to their consoles to play it. How has this video game created such a cross-generational buzz?

image.caption: Lucia and Jason are the protagonists of 'Grand Theft Auto VI': For the first time in the franchise's main titles, gamers can play as a womanImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: "Oh, it's so on now!" is the tagline in the latest trailer for the video game "Grand Theft Auto VI," or "GTA VI" for short.

"GTA VI" is a game of superlatives that's been crashing through records. The hype around it is unparalleled. No game in history has clocked so many pre-orders. It's thought that around 10 million people have already purchased it. There's no denying it: "GTA VI" is a global cultural phenomenon.

A few days before its release on November 19, fans can already start downloading the game. The file is so large that downloading it can take several days, depending on the internet connection. Providers have already registered a significant spike in data traffic.
As soon as the game is unlocked, players can start speeding through the fictional US metropolis of Vice City in a stylish sports car with criminal couple Jason and Lucia.
Miami gets cast as Vice City

To mark the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," its real-life inspiration — Miami — is getting a full-scale "Vice City" makeover. This promotional push includes the Miami Heat basketball team stepping onto the hardwood in custom "Vice City" jerseys for a home game, a local festival featuring artists from the game's official soundtrack, and roadside "Vice City" signage installed across the area.

blocks.caption: Vice City is a fictionalized representation of the US metropolis of MiamiImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: Expectations for "GTA VI" are sky-high. Nearly 5,000 people have been working on the game for more than 10 years. Development costs are estimated at around $1 billion (€900 million).

"Based on those figures alone — as well as the series' extremely successful and popular track record — this can certainly be described as a truly exceptional release," says Rudolf Thomas Inderst, cultural studies scholar and professor of Game Design and Game Studies at Germany's Neu-Ulm University of Applied Sciences.

When such an effort is put into a product, it's only natural for people to expect great things, he adds. Inderst is expecting "GTA VI" to showcase the absolute best of what modern gaming can do across gameplay, storytelling, visuals and tech.
Social satire and gameplay freedom

This video game series has been around for almost three decades, setting new standards through its different versions. A biting satire on US society and the American dream, "GTA" parodies politics, culture and the media.

The game is also renowned for its gameplay freedom and spectacularly staged chaos in a crazy world where players can do whatever they please. Shoot down helicopters with a bazooka, go to the hairdresser's, take a stroll on the beach, go to a nightclub, take part in car races and much more.

blocks.caption: Pure escapism: In Vice City, there's shooting and dancingImage: Rockstar Games/dpa Picture Alliance

blocks.text: What makes it a standout among video games is how its NPCs — non-player characters, those not being controlled by a human player — are brought to life. They respond based on a player's interactions with them, displaying individualized behaviors and traits ranging from fear to hostility. "GTA VI" has an estimated 600,000 animations for the civilians in the fictional state of Leonida.
'Grand Theft Auto,' a long-running hit

"GTA VI" is essentially a huge adult playground, striking a chord across several generations. Millennials grew up with "Grand Theft Auto III," "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City," "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas," and "Grand Theft Auto IV," while Gen Z grew up with "Grand Theft Auto V." Generation Alpha might still be too young for the latest edition, but will likely find ways to play it anyway.

blocks.caption: In 'GTA VI,' Lucia and Jason play a gangster couple; the players' actions determine how close they becomeImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: Social media has certainly played a part in the series' ongoing success, particularly "GTA V" and its multiplayer spin-off, "GTA Online." Numerous content creators stream gameplay sessions on Twitch or YouTube, and particularly funny or crazy gameplay moments end up on TikTok.

At the same time, a dedicated role-play community has grown around the game. Players gather inside the world of "GTA" to act out specific characters, such as taxi drivers, judges or small-time criminals. They invent realistic backstories for their personas, and many even use accents to stay in character.
Perfectionism has its downsides

The hype surrounding "GTA VI" is not only good news for the game itself but could also boost the entire games industry by drawing more people back to their consoles. This is because the boom triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic was followed by studio closures and redundancies. Worldwide, it's estimated that 50,000 people in the games industry have lost their jobs since 2022.

But while publisher Rockstar Games is well-known for the meticulous polish of its titles and attention to detail, the perfectionism so prized by fans also has its drawbacks, especially for those working on the game. Rockstar, like many other game developers, has frequently faced major criticism regarding its labor practices.

blocks.caption: 'GTA' characters can relax at Leonida Keys, but game developers face high-pressure workloads in the lead-up to game releasesImage: Rockstar Games

blocks.text: Former developers report extremely long working hours and a heavy workload that resulted in health issues. Trade unions accuse company managers of employee surveillance, resulting in a culture of workplace stress and low morale.

Coinciding with the launch of Rockstar's largest game to date, the developers behind it are pushing for trade union recognition. That move would give them a collective voice to address working hours, pay, pensions and parental leave. If successful, their campaign could set a major precedent for the wider video game industry, which continues to face challenges around fair labor practices.
This article was originally written in German.
Hooked on video gaming

articles.title: Canadian home sales edged up in October amid overall flat housing market: CREA
articles.summary: Home sales across Canada edged up slightly in October — defying the expectations of some analysts — but remained below levels from October 2025, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association…

image.caption: Home sales edged up nationally in October according to the latest numbers from the Canadian Real Estate Association. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Business

Home sales across Canada edged up slightly in October — defying the expectations of some analysts — but remained below levels from October 2025, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA).
Numbers better than expected, but recent rate hike and overall economy keeping market slow
Home sales across Canada edged up slightly in October but remained below October 2025 levels, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA).
National sales in October were up 0.3 per cent month over month, but still down 10.6 per cent compared to October 2025.

"Not much activity between September and October," said CREA senior economist Shaun Cathcart. "But the remarkable part about that is that it ran counter to … a lot of analysts' — including ours — expectations."

Cathcart expected already slow housing sales to slump into the end of the year after the Bank of Canada raised its benchmark interest rate a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent last month, the first rate change in a year and the first rate hike since 2023.
Real estate experts have predicted the hike will keep cost-conscious potential buyers worried about the potential of rising mortgage payments on the sidelines.
What the new 2.5% interest rate means for Canadians

Cathcart says he still expects sales will remain relatively flat nationally in the coming months while potential buyers perhaps wait to make a purchase until they get a better sense of where rates are going.
"It could be that we only get another maybe one or two hikes, and that once things sort of settle and we get a little bit more certainty next year, you can see the market come back stronger."

The average price of a home in Canada in October was $656,200, down 3.1 per cent from 12 months ago. The markets in Ontario and British Columbia continue to be slow, while the prairies and East Coast have been "hotter" than many people might be aware, Cathcart said.
But with one rate hike already and potentially more to come, he said, "I think you're going to see everyone sort of cooling off a little bit more."
There were 197,000 homes listed through MLS platforms country-wide at the end of October —slightly above the long term average, according to CREA.

articles.title: Trump lands in Philippines for ASEAN, Marcos meeting
articles.summary: United States President Donald Trump arrived in Manila late Tuesday, November 17, to attend a special summit with ASEAN leaders, after skipping the earlier East Asia Summit where the region's leaders…

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 5:57pm

MANILA, Philippines (Updated 6:31 p.m.) — United States President Donald Trump arrived in Manila late Tuesday, November 17, to attend a special summit with ASEAN leaders, after skipping the earlier East Asia Summit where the region's leaders touted the value of standing together amid global uncertainty.
Trump, the last world leader to reach the capital, landed at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport as the 49th ASEAN Summit was drawing to a close.

He is set to join Southeast Asian leaders at an ASEAN-US Special Summit, billed as the final engagement of the three-day meetings. He is also expected to briefly sit down on Tuesday evening with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan under the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, or Quad.
Trump is also scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday, November 18, before flying to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
The visit is Trump's first to the Philippines since November 2017, when he attended the ASEAN Summit hosted by then-president Rodrigo Duterte.

The 21st East Asia Summit, held earlier on Tuesday, brought together the 11 ASEAN member states and eight partner countries, among them Japan, China and Russia. Washington has been a full participant in the forum since 2011.

In his opening remarks at the meeting, Marcos said the summit was entering its third decade at a time "when many of the assumptions that have shaped our region are being tested" and "strategic competition has intensified."

"Conflicts within and beyond our region have disrupted energy, food, trade, and supply chains," Marcos said, urging leaders to adhere to international law and prioritize dialogue amid the "upheaval, uncertainty, and unpredictability of our times."

Trump's absence is no surprise as his attendance in the regional meet has fluctuated even in his first term. In 2017, he left Manila without attending the East Asia Summit plenary, citing delays in the program, and then-secretary of state Rex Tillerson represented the United States; Trump said afterward that he had delivered his prepared remarks at a lunch with the other leaders instead.

In Kuala Lumpur in 2025, Trump witnessed the signing of a Thailand-Cambodia ceasefire on the first day of the ASEAN summit but had left for Japan by the time leaders convened for the wider meetings the following day.
Global uncertainty was a recurring theme in ASEAN and world leaders' speeches from the summit's opening day.

Opening the meetings on Sunday, Marcos said geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, new technologies, climate change and transnational threats were reshaping Southeast Asia "faster than any one country can respond to alone." He said developments in the Middle East earlier this year had put ASEAN nationals at risk and disrupted transport, energy and food supplies across the region.
Much of that disruption traces to the war Trump has waged alongside Israel on Iran, a conflict that Iran retaliated against by blocking trade through the Strait of Hormuz.

The conflict remains unresolved despite attempts at a ceasefire, and Washington has kept a naval blockade and economic pressure campaign against Iran in place. Tehran says it is still waiting for a formal US response to its seven conditions for ending the eight-month war.

With Trump absent for most of the week, other leaders used the meetings to present themselves as advocates of open trade and multilateral cooperation. At Monday's ASEAN-China Summit, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said that although trade restrictions had increased around the world, China, which is ASEAN's biggest trading partner, remained "firmly committed to safeguarding multilateralism and promoting free trade."
Li also said ASEAN and Beijing should "properly handle differences through dialogue [and] jointly oppose foreign interference" — remarks that can be seen as an apparent swipe at Washington.
Trump is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping during the APEC summit in China.

articles.title: Japan offers idle oil tanks for Philippines-led stockpiling plan
articles.summary: Japan is offering its unused oil storage tanks to support a Philippine-led regional stockpiling program.

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 5:57pm

Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi (L) looks at Philippines' President Ferdinand Marcos Jr during the 29th ASEAN-Japan Summit on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Japan has offered to make its unused oil storage tanks available for a Philippine-led regional stockpiling program, as Asian countries seek to build emergency fuel reserves against future supply disruptions.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi announced the proposal Tuesday, Nov. 17, at the Asia Zero Emission Community Summit in Manila, where leaders discussed the region's energy security as supply challenges mounted due to Middle East conflict.
The proposed arrangement would allow participating countries to use spare storage capacity in Japan as part of a joint effort to secure oil supplies during emergencies.
Takaichi also called for stronger cooperation under the Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia, a framework launched in April 2026.
The initiative seeks to strengthen the region's energy resilience alongside its longer-term transition toward carbon neutrality.
Regional oil security task force
Japan's stockpiling offer forms part of broader proposals at the summit, including the creation of an Asia Oil Security Task Force.
Envisioned as an Asian counterpart to the International Energy Agency, the proposed task force would coordinate oil procurement, stockpiling and emergency releases during major supply disruptions.
The framework would have a coordination hub in Tokyo, Japan.

Another proposal, Bridge Asia, seeks to promote joint research and development among participating countries in emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, digital technology and quantum computing.
The initiatives reflect efforts to strengthen regional economic and energy resilience alongside existing commitments to reduce carbon emissions.
Separately, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin signed a memorandum of understanding with the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia on Sunday, November 15.
The agreement provides a framework for technical cooperation and policy support aimed at strengthening Philippine energy security and advancing the country's energy transition.
The Department of Energy is targeting at least 25 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity by 2035 as part of efforts to expand the country's clean energy supply.

articles.title: Tarriela rebuts Chinese scholar's claim that Ayungin Shoal is Chinese territory
articles.summary: Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesperson Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela on Tuesday rejected a Chinese scholar's claim that Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal is Chinese territory, stressing that the disputed…

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 5:53pm

Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesperson Rear Admiral Jay Tristan Tarriela on Tuesday rejected a Chinese scholar's claim that Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal is Chinese territory, stressing that the disputed feature lies within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

Tarriela made the remarks after Dr. Zheng Zhihua of Shanghai Jiao Tong University argued that China was justified in using water cannons against Philippine vessels in the South China Sea, claiming that Beijing was merely defending its territory.

The exchange took place during a discussion on whether the proposed Code of Conduct (COC) between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in the South China Sea should be legally binding.

Zheng said a COC would be ineffective without a fundamental consensus among China and ASEAN member states. He cited what he described as a key disagreement, claiming that the Philippines had been occupying Second Thomas Shoal, which he called Chinese territory, for 27 years.
He also defended China's use of water cannons against Philippine fishing and coast guard vessels operating within the Philippines' EEZ.
"China only uses water cannons as a big power. I think if other countries occupy your land territory, you only use water canals to defend your territory integrity," Zheng said.
Tarriela disputed the professor's assertion.
"I would just like to correct you in saying that China does not have any territorial jurisdiction whatsoever in Second Thomas Shoal," he said.

"The last time I checked, Second Thomas Shoal only has a distance of 125 nautical miles from the Philippines. And it is our exclusive economic zone, not China's," Tarriela added, citing the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which provides for an EEZ extending up to 200 nautical miles from a country's baselines.
Zheng countered by saying: "No country occupied Second Thomas Shoal as easy like Philippines did."
Indonesian scholar Dr. Dewi Fortuna Anwar, meanwhile, said ASEAN should intervene to help defuse tensions in the South China Sea.
Anwar said China should reach out to ASEAN member states rather than assert its power, warning that displays of might would not resolve territorial disputes.
"To jeopardize the goodwills of ASEAN countries over these issues in the South China Sea, I think is, you know, you are shooting your foot," she said.

In July 2016, an arbitral tribunal under the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines in its case against China, rejecting Beijing's expansive claims over much of the South China Sea based on its nine-dash line.
The tribunal also ruled that areas of the Spratly Islands, including Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Reed Bank, are within the Philippines' EEZ and continental shelf.

It further found that China had unlawfully prevented Filipino fishermen from accessing Scarborough Shoal, also known as Panatag Shoal, which it recognized as a traditional fishing ground for both Filipino and Chinese fishermen.
The ruling stemmed from an arbitration case initiated by the Philippines in 2013. China refused to participate in the proceedings and has rejected the ruling.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Trump arrives in Manila for state visit, ASEAN-US Special Summit
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump will also meet with fellow Quad leaders in Manila where protests against Pax Silica and the US war on Iran await him

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – US President Donald Trump arrived in Manila late Tuesday afternoon, November 17, for a state visit and to participate in the ASEAN-US Special Summit and the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) leaders’ summit on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit.

Trump arrived in Manila amid protests from groups opposed to his policies, especially the US war on Iran and his administration’s vaunted Pax Silica initiative. Hundreds had been arrested in relation to the protests that began on November 15, the opening of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.

Before Trump’s late afternoon arrival on Tuesday, ASEAN leaders held meetings with Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, Chinese Premier Li Qiang, and Indian President Narendra Modi, ahead of the annual East Asia Summit.
Trump skipped the East Asia Summit but will join a US-ASEAN Special Summit as well as the Quad leaders’ summit, both scheduled after the conclusion of the ASEAN Summit.

The meeting of the Quad — the US, Japan, Australia, and India — will be Trump’s first and takes place two years after the last gathering of the group, which his predecessor Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative.

It comes just ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping who previously objected to the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing. Quad members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.

On Wednesday, November 18, Trump will have bilateral meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Malacañang, to be followed by a state luncheon in his honor before he departs for the APEC Summit in Shenzen.

Trump’s Asia trip, which also includes a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts in Shenzen, comes after his Republican Party’s defeat in midterm elections and spy allegations that could complicate a fragile trade-war truce between the US and China. – With reports from Reuters/Rappler.com

articles.title: House leader confident Congress will pass 2027 budget on time, avert reenactment
articles.summary: A leader of the House of Representatives expressed confidence that the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 would be approved on time, ruling out the possibility of a reenacted budget.

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 5:30pm
A leader of the House of Representatives expressed confidence that the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 would be approved on time, ruling out the possibility of a reenacted budget.
The House of Representatives approved the proposed 2027 national budget on third and final reading in October. The measure is now undergoing review in the Senate.

"That's the worst thing that can happen, reenactment. I believe we are on the right track in terms of pacing," House Committee on Appropriations vice chairperson Zia Alonto Adiong said in an online interview on Tuesday.
"The Senate is multitasking, doing the impeachment and the budget at the same time. There's nothing to worry about the budget being reenacted because they have set their timeline," he added.
Once the Senate approves its version of the budget, the differences between the House and Senate versions will be reconciled by the bicameral conference committee.
Congress is scheduled to go on Christmas recess on December 19, 2026, with sessions set to resume on January 17, 2027.

Adiong said any possible delay in the budget's approval would likely last only a few days, adding that lawmakers could adjust the session schedule to accommodate the ratification of the bicameral conference committee report.
"The most that we can actually expect as to the possible delay is only a few days. At puwede naman din po magkaroon ng adjustment doon sa session days para po sa ratification ng bicam," he said.
Meanwhile, Adiong said the House is working on establishing a transparency website that would allow the public to monitor government project funding and implementation.
The proposed platform was earlier announced by House Speaker Faustino Dy III.
"Ongoing po yung pagpu-put up nitong website na ito for each, for the succeeding years to come," Alonto Adiong said.

He added that the public would be able to access information on projects during the budget season, including their identification in each congressional district and their subsequent implementation. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Indian woman gang-raped while pregnant in 2002 'heartbroken' after two perpetrators bailed
articles.summary: Bilkis Bano has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" at the top court order and vowed to fight back.

blocks.text: The article has details that some readers may find disturbing

A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.
Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back.
The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.
All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order.

In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.
The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".
On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken".

"She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary."
Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".
The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.
Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.
When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child.
They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she'd told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.

items: How a Gujarat riot victim stood up to her rapists
India Supreme Court cancels release of 2002 riots rapists
India PM Modi's government okayed rapists' release

blocks.text: Her attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.
Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.
Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.

Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.
In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief".
"I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said.

"For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again."
Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives".

"I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."

Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.
In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

articles.title: Mozambique opposition leader faces trial over deadly 2024 election unrest
articles.summary: Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges over 2024 post-election protests that left hundreds of people dead.

blocks.text: Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.
Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.
Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.
Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.
The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.
"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.

Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.
Prosecutors accuse Mondlane of encouraging demonstrations that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security.
The charges include publicly glorifying criminal acts, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit crimes and offences linked to terrorism.
He could face up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge.
Mondlane has rejected the accusations, insisting that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency rather than encouraging violence.
His party, the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), has described the prosecution as politically motivated.
The Supreme Court has denied allegations of political interference in the proceedings.
A heavy deployment of police has been seen patrolling around the Supreme Court and major streets in Maputo ahead of the trial.

In a statement issued on Monday, Mozambique's police appealed to citizens to "preserve tolerance and peaceful coexistence," adding that the right to demonstrate must be exercised strictly within the limits of the law.
Police also pledged to protect people and property while acting preventively and proportionately in accordance with the rule of law.
The court has only granted access to selected media organisations, sparking criticism from journalists and press freedom campaigners.
Court officials say the restrictions are necessary because of limited seating capacity in the courtroom, but critics argue they undermine transparency in a case of significant public interest.
The proceedings are expected to be heard by five judges, with witnesses called by both the prosecution and defence.
Political observers warn that the trial could reignite tensions in a country still struggling to recover from the violence and deep political divisions that followed the 2024 elections.

articles.title: Alleged coercion of VP Sara's ex-staffer a 'coordinated social media activity' — NBI
articles.summary: The claims of supposed coercion of the former staff of Vice President Sara Duterte are a coordinated social media activity, according to National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag.

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 5:07pm
Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte (front R) leaves court after posting bail in Quezon City, suburban Manila on September 5, 2026.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — The claims of supposed coercion of the former staff of Vice President Sara Duterte are a coordinated social media activity, according to National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag.

In a Zoom press conference on November 17, Matibag said that the agency only observed simultaneous postings across social media platforms about the narrative, which points to a coordinated effort to spread the narrative online.
"Wala kaming na-receive except maraming nagpasa nung mga it appears to be coordinated behavior sa social media na sabay-sabay na nag-post na merong ganitong pangyayari," Matibag said.
(We have not received anything, except many people forwarded what appears to be coordinated behavior on social media, simultaneously posting that such an incident happened.)
"Sana there should be a formal report so we can investigate. Kung ayaw sa amin, there is PNP," he added.
(Hopefully, there will be a formal report so we can investigate. If they don't want to file it with us, there is the PNP.)
Matibag added that the bureau has received zero formal complaints or referrals regarding the alleged incident.
Earlier, in a message to Philstar.com, Matibag said that if they feel the urgency to report the incident, Duterte's camp should file a complaint.
Without any clear documentation or concrete evidence, the NBI chief dismissed the online allegations as mere rumors.
"Well, overall reaction eh pagka wala tayong malinaw na document of evidence, I will borrow the words nila na ginagamit ay chismis lang yan," Matibag said.
(Well, as an overall reaction, if we do not have a clear document of evidence, I will borrow the words they use—that is just gossip.)

The first Facebook post came in the morning on Tuesday from former human rights lawyer and presidential spokesperson Harry Roque, who claimed that the vice president received a message from what appeared to be the account of a former household staff member containing a "desperate plea for help and rescue in Manila."

He added that the sender claimed to be under the custody or control of certain individuals who allegedly warned of a threat to the former staffer's life and tried to force them to sign a document, which they refused to execute.

Also in his post, Roque likened the alleged incident to that of Jefry Tupas, claiming that NBI agents had previously told Tupas on Sept. 29, 2026, of threats to his life before attempting to bring him to Manila.
Hours later, the same Facebook post was copy-pasted by lawyer Paolo Duterte, who is one of the spokespersons of the vice president.

Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City 1st District) at 10:38 a.m. then called the actions a tactic to intimidate and pressure individuals into signing documents and acting as witnesses to fabricate a case against his sister.

Aside from the impeachment trial, Duterte is also facing a grave threat charge before a Quezon City Regional Trial Court over her threats in October and November 2024 press conferences against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.

The NBI is also investigating alleged irregularities in the properties of the vice president and her husband, Manases Carpio, which are indicated in their Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth.

articles.title: House impeachment trial spokesman Adiong urges Sara Duterte camp to report alleged threat
articles.summary: House Impeachment Trial spokesperson Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong on Tuesday called on the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte to report to the authorities the alleged threat received by one…

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 5:05pm

House Impeachment Trial spokesperson Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong on Tuesday called on the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte to report to the authorities the alleged threat received by one of her former household staff.

Adiong said this after Duterte's spokesperson, Atty. Paolo Panelo, said the vice president received a message yesterday from the staff member, asking for help and rescue. The whereabouts of the former household staff member is unknown.
"The course of action that has to be taken as far as this issue is concerned is to go to the authorities and file for a missing person report," Adiong said in an interview.

On Panelo's claim that the incident may be part of the Marcos Administration's campaign against the vice president, Alonto Adiong said, "I don't expect anything from their side to talk about how law and order or rule of law is being implemented in this country."
"They would really twist, for example, or make some issues out of it by presenting that the Marcos administration or this administration is doing, you know, a witch hunt, for example," Adiong said.

"So this kind of statements, I guess, is something that we expect from their camp. And I hope that they can finally, since they already have those allegations, I hope they can finally bring this up to the proper authorities," he added.

Adiong said that this could be meant "to segue from political issue to divert the attention of the public from the ongoing trial." He said the defense witnesses have failed to affect the evidence the prosecution has presented.

He said the defense dug itself a deeper hole after a witness said Duterte received a monthly allowance or income from Gen Corp, "which is essentially what we have been accusing the Vice President of." –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Youth unemployment plan could cut welfare bill before election, says Milburn, but overall savings will take years – UK politics live
articles.summary: Long-awaited report on Neets will be published this morning as author acknowledges that there will be initial costs

blocks.text: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6%, as government prepares to release Milburn report
The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government prepares to release the Alan Milburn report on the youth jobs crisis, Phillip Inman reports.
Alan Milburn says youth unemployment plan could cut welfare bill, but overall savings will take years

Good morning. Few government reports have been as long-awaited and well-trailed as the Alan Milburn report into youth unemployment, or Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), that is finally being published this morning. The title, From a Welfare State to a Working State, gives a clue as to the extent of Milburn’s ambition and, if it gets implemented in full, it will be remembered as one of the landmark social reforms of the 21st century (so far).

And even if Milburn only achieves 50% of what he wants (which, sadly, is probably quite a good success rate for the authors of independent government reports), he will change Britain significantly, as Polly Toynbee argues in a must-read column about the report today. She says:

double quotation markThere will, no doubt, be protest from right and left. But never has a policy been so pitch-rolled to flatten critics and sceptics with undeniable evidence that it will be to the good. There is a cornucopia of plans for schools, colleges, the NHS, councils and early years education. Ideas come from visits to see what works elsewhere, notably the Netherlands and Denmark. Seeing proportionally far fewer Neets in those countries, Milburn asked what they did about school and college drop-outs. “They didn’t understand that term,” he tells me. In those countries, if children start to struggle with school attendance, “they go straight round to find them and work out their problem. Here they disappear.” Politically, this duty will fall on local mayors (or councils, where mayors have not yet been introduced). Their colossal task is to pull together schools, FE colleges, jobcentres, NHS services and local employers. Heaving them out of their silos to collaborate will test mayoral devolution to its limits. With extra funding comes accountability for creating a continuous decline in the number of Neets in their area. Everywhere, this will be delivered through youth hubs – welcoming places, “not jobcentres where they’re met by security guards, but places only for young people,” Milburn tells me. Last week he visited a model hub in Liverpool, Merseyside Youth Association. Hiring and training a new cohort of work coaches and advisers has begun, so hubs can offer supported internships, short flexi-jobs to ease people into work and experience for those with none on their CVs. Incentives to employers to hire them may include cuts to employers’ national insurance contributions for those aged 21-24 in retail and hospitality. Ordinary earners under 21 are already NI-free … It’s for Labour and Milburn, who will remain in post to oversee all of this, to prove, with falling Neet numbers, the value of good social investment. If even half these plans work, that will be a great social advance – a generational shift from appeasing the old to finally directing hope and resources towards the young. And it will be about time.

The full report is being published this morning. But it won’t contain any surprises – Milburn has been talking about his proposals for weeks now, and all the main ideas are already in the public domain. Here is our overnight story by Richard Partington, Kiran Stacey and Aletha Adu.

So far, none of the reaction from the charity sector has been particularly hostile. The opposition parties have generally welcomed the bits of the plan that overlap with their own policies, while criticising the rest. But, for the government, the reaction that matters the most will come in the Commons, when Labour MPs get the chance to say what they think.

Milburn has been giving interviews this morning. And he has claimed that, under his plan, the government could start to save money from the welfare budget before the end of this parliament. This is an important pledge because John Healey, the chancellor, was criticised recently by the Tories for failing to propose cutting benefits before the next election.
Milburn told Times Radio:

double quotation markWe should be doing that. We can get the benefits bill down. And by the way, we can do that quickly. We can start in this parliament to get savings from welfare. But what we’ve got to do is start creating opportunities and support for young people.

But those savings would not at first offset the extra government spending his plan would require. Milburn says his proposals would require “an immediate upfront payment” of £500m in the next financial year.
On the Today programme, Milburn argued that, over time, his plan would save money. He explained:

double quotation markWe can either get the benefits bill down through crude cuts. And when that happens, all that then happens is more young people are in destitution and poverty and frankly will show up somewhere else on the ledger in more housing costs or health costs or crime costs. Or we can do it through more jobs. And my view is that it’s got to be more jobs. And over time then, what happens by the time the 10-year programme gets to a conclusion, we will have saved about £13.8bn in welfare.

Milburn was referring to the amount saved from the welfare budget. His plans would require extra spending in other areas, and his plan would involve around £5.8bn a year of funding by 2036-37, offset by £3.6bn of welfare savings and £2.4bn of extra tax revenue from people in work.

When it was put to him that in the short term, his plan “costs, doesn’t save”, Milburn replied: “Correct.” And when it was put to him that the “crossover point” when overall savings would overtake overall costs would only happen after 10 years, Milburn replied: “That’s when it happens.”
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Andy Burnham chairs cabinet, where Alan Milburn will speak about his youth unemployment report.
9.30am: The Department for Work and Pensions publishes quarterly universal credit figures.
Morning: Kemi Badenoch and Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, are on a visit in London.
10.30am: Marsha de Cordova MP and Sandro Gozi MEP, co-chairs of the UK-EU Parliamentary Partnership Assembly, hold a press conference after its meeting in London.
11.30am: Milburn holds a press conference to mark the publication of his report.
11.30am: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 12.30pm: Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, is due to give a statement to MPs about the Milburn report.

articles.title: 5 European countries want to start deporting migrants to Rwanda, despite concerns from human rights groups
articles.summary: Five European countries have embarked on a deal with Rwanda to take in migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected. They are hoping the scheme acts as a deterrent, but a similar plan in Britain…

image.caption: From left: Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner, Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta, Greek Minister for Migration and Asylu

blocks.text: World·Analysis

Five European countries have embarked on a deal with Rwanda to take in migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected. They are hoping the scheme acts as a deterrent, but a similar plan in Britain was quashed after the court called it unlawful.
Countries working with Rwanda to set up 'return hub' for migrants who don't have legal right to remain in EU

In one of his first acts as Britain's prime minister, Keir Starmer in 2024 quashed the U.K. government's controversial plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, saying it was "dead and buried before it started."
Now, five European countries are trying to resurrect a similar scheme.

Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Greece announced Monday that they are working with Rwanda to set up a "return hub" for migrants who do not have the legal right to remain in the European Union.

"We need to take back control of our borders," said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen during a joint news conference in Vienna. "What we are pushing for is a more sustainable and, I will also say, a more orderly asylum and migration system."
Those sent to Rwanda will be given the chance to integrate and settle there or another nation that grants them the legal right to stay — or return to their home country.

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at a joint news conference that the EU countries' Rwanda deportation hub plan would be a 'game changer' for illegal migration. (Helmut Fohringer/APA/AFP/Getty Images)
Mounting political pressure

The plan, which some EU officials have dubbed a "game changer," is part of a hardening stance toward asylum seekers. It comes as many European governments face growing pressure from voters and rival far-right political parties to show they can control migration.
In September, a regional election victory by Germany’s far-right, anti-immigration party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), was widely seen as a symbol of changing public sentiment toward migration.

Over the past few years, asylum claims in Europe have been dropping, and experts point to a combination of factors, including changes in government policy and the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in Syria in 2024. In 2023, there were more than a million first-time asylum applications. Last year, the annual figure dropped to just under 670,000, according to data from the European Union.

Migrants board a coast guard boat from a Frontex vessel, to be transferred to the port of Kaloi Limenes, following a rescue operation on the island of Crete, Greece, on Nov. 9. (Stefanos Rapanis/Reuters)
Britain's failed experiment
When Britain first unveiled its Rwanda partnership in 2022, then-prime minister Boris Johnson pitched it as necessary to stop boats full of asylum seekers from crossing the English Channel.
The year prior, there were nearly 50,000 asylum claims in the U.K.

Under the British plan, people could be sent to Rwanda while British authorities processed their asylum claims. Under the proposed European arrangement, the east-central African nation would only take in those whose asylum applications have already been rejected and who cannot be sent back to their home countries because of a lack of co-operation.

For Rwanda, proponents argue that the agreement presents an economic opportunity, and European officials are framing the country as an ideal place for a "second chance." Critics dispute that characterization, arguing Rwanda has a track record of repression. Amnesty International said that without scrutiny the Rwanda deal could become a "black hole for human rights."

Britain's then-home secretary Suella Braverman, left, and Rwanda's then-minister of infrastructure Ernest Nsabimana, right, lay bricks at a housing development for migrants in the Rwandan capital Kigali on March 19, 2023. Britain eventually scrapped a controversial plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda. (The Associated Press)
In a joint statement, 47 organizations urged the countries to scrap the Rwanda plan, arguing there are insufficient legal safeguards and no monitoring system to eliminate the risk of rights abuses.
In 2025 — two years after Britain's Supreme Court ruled the U.K.'s Rwanda plan unlawful — the U.S. struck its own deal with the country to accept up to 250 migrants.
No hard numbers

When European officials unveiled their agreement during Monday's news conference in Vienna, they said they hope to send the first people to Rwanda by the end of 2027, though they did not specify how many people in total would be sent there.

The five countries are billing the plan as a pilot project, insisting it will act as a deterrent to prevent people from travelling — sometimes thousands of kilometres — to reach Europe in the first place.

"As everybody knows, criminal organizations are making billions of euros on human smuggling, and too many lives are lost at sea," said Frederiksen. "We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders."
In her speech, Frederiksen said some European leaders have been working toward this kind of initiative for "eight or nine years."

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta says he believes that under the 'return hub' plan, asylum seekers in Europe may opt to return to their countries of origin without going through Rwanda at all. He added that Kigali was not planning for 'thousands' of people to stay in the east-central African nation. (Helmut Fohringer/APA/AFP/Getty Images)
New EU rule

The announcement of the Rwanda hub comes a month and a half after the Council of the European Union greenlit a new policy, the EU Return Regulation, which opened the door to setting up migrant hubs outside Europe.
The rules stipulate that unaccompanied minors cannot be deported and that hubs can only be created in countries that respect "international human rights and the principles of international law."
Clémentine de Montjoye, a senior researcher in the Africa division at Human Rights Watch, called the plan "utterly deplorable," in part because of what she calls a stunning contradiction.

Europe has repeatedly voiced concerns about Rwanda’s human rights record and its support for M23, an armed group accused of committing war crimes in the eastern region of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
De Montjoye pointed out that Germany even reduced its aid to Rwanda last year because of its role in the conflict, which has displaced hundreds of thousands of people.

A bicycle taxi driver looks on while waiting for customers at a busy junction near a market in Kigali, on July 16, 2024. The east African nation is set to host a deportation hub for failed asylum seekers from five European countries. (Luis Tato/AFP/Getty Images)
Now, Germany and four other countries are trying to frame Rwanda as a land of opportunity.

"The question is: What kind of due diligence has been done by these five countries?" De Montjoye told CBC News from Nairobi, Kenya. "It's very concerning that the risk of human rights harms are being kind of swept under the carpet in order to present an image of coming up with solutions."
'Fig leaf' of deterrence

Outlining the motivations for creating the hub, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said European countries are hampered because countries of origin often do not co-operate when it comes to taking back rejected asylum seekers.
According to statistics from the Mixed Migration Centre, which operates under the Danish Refugee Council, only one in five people ordered to leave Europe actually do so.

A demonstrator holds a placard reading 'Stop EU-Rwanda-deal,' on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development on Monday in Vienna. (Radek Mica/AFP/Getty Images)
Roberto Forin, the centre's deputy director, says there is a need to manage migration in a more orderly way, but believes the Rwanda deal will act only as a "fig leaf" rather than a real deterrent.
He says smugglers will adapt, and asylum seekers who feel they have no alternative will continue to make risky journeys, even if the odds of being allowed to stay are lower.
"This is more about politics than migration policy," he told CBC News from Vienna. "Governments, actually across the political spectrum, have made a tough border as part of their promises to voters."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Briar Stewart is a CBC correspondent, based in London. During her nearly two decades with CBC, she has reported across Canada and internationally. She can be reached at briar.stewart@cbc.ca or on X @briarstewart.

articles.title: Jury in coroner's inquest hears how woman from Alberta died in northwestern Ontario
articles.summary: The first day of a coroner's inquest into the death of a woman at Lake of the Woods District Hospital in Kenora, Ont., took place via video conference on Monday. Here's what members of the jury heard…

image.caption: A photo of the late Kaylee Martha Dallas Crowchild. Her mother, Michelle Crowchild, says Kaylee was a kind and loving person who enjoyed dancing, music and helping out around the house. The 29-year-old member of Tsuut’ina Nation in southern Alberta died on Sept. 20, 2022 at Lake of the Woods Distric

blocks.text: Thunder Bay·In-Depth

The first day of a coroner's inquest into the death of a woman at Lake of the Woods District Hospital in Kenora, Ont., took place via video conference on Monday. Here's what members of the jury heard about the late Kaylee Martha Dallas Crowchild of Tsuut’ina Nation in southern Alberta and how she ended up in northwestern Ontario.
Kaylee Martha Dallas Crowchild of Tsuut’ina Nation died on Sept. 20, 2022
WARNING: This story contains references to sexual assault and suicide. Resources can be found at the bottom of this story.
Michelle Crowchild says her daughter, Kaylee Martha Dallas Crowchild, was a kind and loving person who would give her last dollar to someone in need.
A coroner’s inquest into Kaylee’s death began on Monday. The 29-year-old was a member of Tsuut’ina Nation, a Dene community about 40 kilometres southwest of Calgary, Alberta.
The jury heard that Kaylee died on Sept. 20, 2022 at Lake of the Woods District Hospital in Kenora, Ont., after being transferred from the Kenora District Jail.
Inquests are mandatory under the Coroners Act when a person dies in custody. The proceedings are being held via video conference.

In a coroner’s inquest, witnesses provide information about the circumstances surrounding a person’s death, after which a five-person jury is tasked with identifying who died, when and where the person died, their medical cause of death and means of death.

Jurors will then classify how the death happened: due to natural causes, accident, homicide, suicide or undetermined. While they cannot make any legal findings or lay blame on anyone, they may make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.
The Kenora District Jail in northwestern Ontario is seen in this screenshot from Google Maps. (Google Streetview)

On Monday, the jury heard that Kaylee’s inquest is expected to focus on suicide screening within the Kenora District Jail, policies in place in 2022 during the COVID-19 pandemic, and cultural supports for Indigenous inmates.

Between 2023-2024, more than 30 per cent of adult inmates at provincial and federal correctional facilities were Indigenous, despite the fact that Indigenous people comprised only four per cent of Canada’s population at this time, according to Statistics Canada.
She was a daughter, a mother, family member, friend and community member whose life encompassed experiences beyond the events that brought us here today.Makenzie Chan, inquest counsel

“While this data is important to acknowledge, it is equally important to remember that Miss Crowchild is more than the circumstances in which she found herself in at the Kenora Jail,” said Makenzie Chan, who is serving as inquest counsel alongside Robert Kozak and Jenna Simpson.
“She was a daughter, a mother, family member, friend and community member whose life encompassed experiences beyond the events that brought us here today.”
Mother asks jury to think of her 'as a person'
Jurors heard that Kaylee was one of seven siblings. She loved dancing and music, especially the Spice Girls, and enjoyed cooking, cleaning and helping her mother, Michelle Crowchild said.
The jury heard of Kaylee’s struggles in her youth. She was sexually assaulted by a family member at a young age, something her mother only found out after her death.
Residents of Black Bear Crossing in Tsuut’ina Nation were forced to evacuate in 2006 due to asbestos and other health concerns at the former military barracks. (CBC)

In 2006 when she was 13 years old, her family was forced to evacuate from their home at Black Bear Crossing in Tsuut’ina Nation and leave all their belongings behind. The former military barracks was deemed uninhabitable due to asbestos and other health concerns.
During the eight months her family lived in a hotel, Kaylee kept running away, her mother said. Around this time, she started using alcohol and drugs, and eventually ended up living on the streets.
In the days leading up to her death, Kaylee ended up in hospital in Brandon, Man. Her mother was told she refused treatment and was seen leaving with two men.
On Sept. 14, 2022, she was arrested in Dryden, Ont. She told police she was sexually assaulted the day before, the jury heard.
Michelle Crowchild says Kaylee had never left Alberta before this point. Her family believes she may have been the victim of human trafficking.
Kaylee was eligible for release from jail the day after her arrest but needed $100 in bail money, the jury heard.

items: Coroner's inquest into Alberta woman's death in Kenora, Ont., slated to start on Monday
Inquest into 2022 death of Alberta woman who died in Kenora, Ont., set for November

blocks.text: Her mother was told she died by suicide six days after being taken into custody.
“I still don't want to believe that,” Michelle Crowchild said. “She loved her children too much. She loved her family too much.”
Kaylee leaves behind a 10-year-old son, who is being raised by her mother, and a six-year-old daughter who has been placed in care.

blocks.text: Michelle Crowchild told the jury she hopes they think of her daughter as a person and not just as someone who was dealing with addiction.
“She was a mom, she was a young girl and she was a member of our community and loved dearly,” she said.
The inquest is expected to last six days and hear from about 11 witnesses. People can watch a livestream of the proceedings online here.

articles.title: ASEAN leaders sign new power grid deal. What’s next for Philippines?
articles.summary: Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon Garin says the ADB and World Bank have 'indicated their interest in financing' regional power grid connections, which could require hundreds of billions of dollars…

blocks.text: ASEAN. Energy ministers from different ASEAN member-states pose ahead of discussions on regional energy issues, on October 7, 2026.
ASEAN

Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon Garin says the ADB and World Bank have 'indicated their interest in financing' regional power grid connections, which could require hundreds of billions of dollars in investment

items: All 11 ASEAN countries have signed an Enhanced Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on the ASEAN Power Grid, aiming for an interconnected electricity network to facilitate cross-border electricity trade.

The agreement focuses on infrastructure planning, policy development, and financing, with significant potential benefits for the Philippines, including improved electricity reliability and reduced reliance on fossil fuels.

Challenges include the need for substantial investments in infrastructure and the integration of power markets, with ASEAN targeting fully integrated operations by 2045, although no firm construction timetable has been established.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Southeast Asian nations have long dreamed of an interconnected electricity network. Now, they are one step closer after all 11 ASEAN countries completed the signing of a power grid agreement that could eventually allow them to buy and sell electricity across borders.
The Enhanced Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on the ASEAN Power Grid officially entered into force upon completion of its signing on Sunday, November 15, during the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila.

According to ASEAN, the agreement “covers cooperation on infrastructure planning, institutional arrangements, policy and regulatory development, and access to financing, including for overland transmission lines and subsea power cables.” (Watch ADB’s brief explainer video below:

The agreement builds on discussions during the 48th ASEAN Summit in Cebu last May, when leaders pushed for greater regional energy connectivity, particularly through submarine power cables connecting the region’s island economies. This continued during the ASEAN energy ministers’ meeting in Manila last October, when all member countries at the time reached a consensus on the agreement.
With all ASEAN countries now manifesting their support for an interconnected grid, the proposal now moves down to the more detailed technical, legal, and financial levels of discussion.

blocks.caption: Rappler Recap: Myanmar, South China Sea among issues as 49th ASEAN Summit opens

blocks.text: For the Philippines, the benefits could be significant. Connecting to neighboring countries could allow the country to import electricity when domestic supplies are tight. Beyond improving reliability, it could also help move the Philippines’ away from expensive and dirty fossil fuel generation. (READ: Solar for whom? What Philippines can learn from Pakistan’s rooftop boom)
But connecting the grids will be neither cheap nor easy.

The Philippines itself operates three major electricity grids, Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, which are now interconnected but still face transmission constraints. It was only in 2023 that the P52-billion Mindanao-Visayas Interconnection Project was energized, allowing electricity to flow between the two regions.

Even this year, the Visayas and Mindanao grids have repeatedly been placed under yellow and red alerts, with parts of the Visayas experiencing rotational power outages. These shortages were caused mainly by power plant outages, compounded by transmission constraints that capped the amount of electricity the Visayas could import from Luzon.
Connecting the Philippines to the rest of ASEAN would no doubt require another major investment in submarine cables, alongside improvements to domestic transmission infrastructure.

The costs could be substantial. According to the International Energy Agency, ASEAN would need around $27 billion in investment in cross-border power interconnections from 2025 to 2040, on top of more than $300 billion needed to expand and modernize domestic electricity grids. ASEAN’s own estimate is even higher, at $764 billion covering both power generation and transmission through 2045, assuming high adoption of renewable energy.

The regional bloc knows this well, which is why its enhanced MOU encourages pooling resources among governments, the private sector, and financial institutions to finance power grid projects. This is complemented by the ASEAN Power Grid Financing Initiative, which brings together ASEAN, the Asian Development Bank, and the World Bank to help prepare projects and mobilize funding.

Energy Undersecretary Felix William Fuentebella said that investors will view the signing of all ASEAN members in the enhanced MOU as a strong positive sign, which could unlock “big amounts of investments” and pave the way for more detailed feasibility studies on interconnections. Energy Secretary Garin also said that the ADB, World Bank, and other development-focused financial institutions have “indicated their interest in financing this” depending on the project proposal.

blocks.caption: ASEAN leaders sign new power grid deal. What’s next for Philippines?

blocks.text: Another major challenge could be power market integration, which ASEAN said would follow a “voluntary, stepwise approach” that takes into account policies, laws, and regulations of the participating countries.

“It will be by steps, voluntary – because we won’t be forcing any country that will not participate,” Garin told Rappler in a press conference on Tuesday, November 17. “But with the signature of everyone in the enhanced MOU, that’s a clear indication already of their participation.”
ASEAN is targeting fully integrated regional electricity grid operations by 2045, although individual connections could be developed earlier.

However, for now, no firm construction timetable has been set, with ASEAN acknowledging that “further development of technical, regulatory and commercial frameworks will be essential to translate this foundation into bankable investments.”

On November 15, the Philippines’ Department of Energy also separately signed a two-year research agreement with the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, which includes technical studies supporting the Philippines’ participation in the regional grid. – Rappler.com
