articles.title: European-made pesticides named in 1,605 poisoning reports in Brazil last year
articles.summary:
About a third of cases involved chemicals banned for use on EU farms, according to investigation by Unearthed and Public Eye

Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in…

blocks.text: Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in more than 1,600 poisoning reports in Brazil last year, an investigation has found.

About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used.

Analysis of Brazilian health ministry data by Unearthed and Public Eye in a report published on Tuesday found that of 2,857 poisoning reports that named an identifiable agricultural product, 1,605 named brands sold by European pesticide companies.

Farm workers in Brazil have described their flesh rotting, skin burning, difficulty breathing and vomiting after using the chemicals at work, according to the report. A small number have died accidentally or killed themselves by drinking the pesticides.

Under Brazilian law, reports must be submitted by healthcare professionals to Brazil’s national disease notification system in all suspected pesticide poisoning cases. These reports can be marked “confirmed” poisoning or “exposure” only by the doctor or nurse who saw the patient.

blocks.caption: A worker in protective gear rinses gloves under water near a pesticide warning sign in Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Clinicians sometimes record cases as exposure when they lack the training or support to confirm a diagnosis, but are presented with a patient who says they have been exposed to pesticides or present symptoms of pesticide poisoning. Laboratory confirmation is rare, so recording a diagnosis of “confirmed” poisoning usually depends on clinical judgment.
Experts say clinicians can be reluctant to confirm cases because of a lack of training or support. A brand being named in a poisoning report is not proof that it caused poisoning or death.

“The insufficient training of healthcare professionals to recognise and manage these cases is a major limiting factor,” said Vanda Garibotti, a public health biologist at the State Centre for Health Surveillance in Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil.
High staff turnover and a lack of institutional support meant poisoning cases were rarely confirmed through laboratory tests and often relied on clinical judgment, Garibotti added.

In more than 6,700 medical reports involving agricultural pesticides last year, 2,857 named an identifiable product. Of those, 1,420 were classified as confirmed poisonings. A further 1,108 were classified as exposures; for the remainder the classification was unknown or other diagnoses.

Some of the products are made in Britain. Reglone is the most frequently cited UK-made weedkiller. It contains diquat, a chemical that was banned in the UK in 2020 after experts concluded it posed a high risk to people living near fields where it was sprayed. Diquat is also found in other pesticides.

Despite the usage ban, Reglone is still manufactured by the Swiss-headquartered pesticides company Syngenta at its factory in Huddersfield for export to countries with more permissive regulations, including Brazil.

blocks.caption: A mass is held in honour of Nelson Castoldi in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Nelson Castoldi died last year after accidentally ingesting Reglone on his family farm in Rio Grande do Sul. To save money, his family had bought the weedkiller in bulk, decanting a single litre into an empty cola bottle to avoid hauling a heavy 20-litre canister into the fields.

Working under the scorching sun, Castoldi mistook the black chemical for a soft drink and took a sip. Though he spat it out immediately, the chemical caused his kidneys to fail before attacking his lungs. He died two days later.

“We fell apart,” Ivan Castoldi said of his father’s death. “Four months after our father passed away, our mother also passed away. She cried day and night. She became depressive and had a stroke. She was left alone.
“That poison, Reglone, should be banned in Brazil,” he added. “Not because of what happened to us, but because of its toxicity.”
The Brazilian health ministry recorded 75 cases involving diquat last year, compared with 36 over the five years from 2018 to 2022.

The investigation found Reglone was specifically named in 44 reports, including four deaths. Of those cases, 26 were classified as confirmed poisonings and the rest were classified as exposure, unknown, or adverse reaction.
Dormex, a pesticide manufactured in Germany by Alzchem and distributed in Brazil by the German chemical company BASF, is another product workers said injured them or made them ill.

blocks.caption: Sidnei Souza de Oliveira, 49, suffered a severe injury after a jug of Dormex spilled on his leg while he was filling a sprayer. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Sidnei Souza de Oliveira, 49, suffered a severe injury after a jug of Dormex spilled on his leg while he was filling a sprayer. The handle broke as he was transferring the chemical into the tank. At first, his leg turned red, and he continued spraying.

He carried on working for four days before going to hospital. “After 15 days, my leg was black. Chunks of flesh were falling off,” Oliveira said. A doctor said the injury was serious and had to remove dead tissue to stop it spreading towards the bone.

Oliveira said the protective trousers supplied by his employer were thin and allowed the chemical to seep through. He said he had been afraid of losing his job if he stayed away from work for too long.

Dormex contains cyanamide, which was banned from use in the EU in 2008 because of concerns about its effects on human health, particularly among farm workers spraying the chemical. Analysis shows the Brazilian health ministry database recorded 17 confirmed poisonings involving Dormex last year.

Finale, a BASF product identified in the investigation, contains glufosinate, which was banned in the EU in 2018. Roundup – a glyphosate-based weedkiller manufactured by the German chemical company Bayer – was frequently cited in Brazilian poisoning reports, including 12 deaths.

Across all the poisoning reports identified by the investigation as involving products sold by European companies, there were 32 reported deaths. Of these cases, 31 were classified as confirmed poisonings, and 26 were recorded as suicides.

Syngenta products were cited 425 times in the poisoning reports, and BASF 179 times. The company figures are not mutually exclusive: some poisoning reports named products sold by more than one manufacturer.
Nina Schrank, a senior campaigner at Greenpeace UK, said the findings were a “deadly double standard”.

“If a pesticide is too dangerous to use in Britain, it should be too dangerous to export. Ministers must stop allowing Britain to be part of a production line for toxic chemicals that are putting lives at risk overseas.”

blocks.caption: Empty pesticide containers in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: The EU’s pesticide approval system requires chemicals to meet strict standards for human and animal health and the environment. Diquat has been banned on EU and UK farms since 2019 and 2020 respectively, after experts concluded it posed a high risk to workers, people living nearby and birds. Cyanamide was withdrawn after an assessment found exposure among agricultural operators could exceed safe levels. Glufosinate, meanwhile, is classified in the EU as toxic to reproduction, meaning it can harm fertility or the development of unborn children.

Suicide prevention is also a factor. A 2020 study found national bans on highly hazardous pesticides could be a cost-effective intervention for reducing the number of people who kill themselves in countries with a high burden of suicides attributable to pesticides.

A Syngenta spokesperson said almost half the Brazilian cases attributed to the company were not classified as confirmed poisonings, adding: “Public Eye and Unearthed are aware of this but have explicitly chosen to disregard the dataset’s final classification.” The company accused the investigation of disregarding the dataset’s final classifications and identified “numerous other inconsistencies” that it said raised “serious concerns” that the evidence was “being selectively interpreted to support a predetermined conclusion”.
“There are real people behind these statistics. Every genuine case of poisoning matters, and every family affected deserves our concern,” the spokesperson added.

Syngenta said Brazil had its own “robust regulatory system” and that products banned in Europe could still be independently assessed and legally registered in the country, citing differences in crops, growing conditions and pest pressures. It said it trained 95,000 people in Brazil in the safe use of its products in 2025, including through free online courses.

blocks.caption: Pesticide are sprayed in an apple orchard in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Photograph: Marcelo Curia/Greenpeace

blocks.text: Bayer said its products were safe when used according to label instructions, citing what it described as rigorous testing and assessments by global health authorities. The company said it took pesticide poisoning seriously but questioned the reliability of the data, arguing that products and circumstances of exposure had not been independently verified, some chemicals may have been incorrectly identified and symptoms such as headaches and skin irritation could have other causes.
It said “Roundup” was “widely used as a generic term” that could refer to weedkillers made by other manufacturers or counterfeit products.

The company said it provided training on the safe handling and use of pesticides, including protective equipment, and that its programmes reached more than 4 million people globally in 2025. It also argued that a pesticide being banned in the EU did not necessarily mean it was unsafe, saying other countries had robust regulatory systems that took account of local agricultural conditions.

It added: “While the data presented helps to provide information on broad trends of exposure, the data has limitations and warrants caution when drawing conclusions, particularly when looking at individual cases.”
BASF said it was deeply concerned by reports of poisoning that might be linked to its products, adding that it took all such incidents seriously.

A spokesperson said publicly available information suggested some incidents might have involved the intentional ingestion of crop protection products, describing such acts as “deliberate misuse” of products intended exclusively for agricultural use.

BASF said it had global and local procedures to assess and investigate incidents potentially involving its products, and worked with authorities and experts where appropriate to understand cases and identify ways to prevent similar incidents. It said it invested in education and training to promote the safe handling and use of its products, with initiatives in Brazil reaching more than 14,475 participants in 2025.
The company said it was confident in the safety of its products when used in accordance with label instructions and applicable regulatory standards.

It added that Brazilian law required crop protection products to be handled and applied only by authorised and properly trained individuals, and said it took its responsibility for ensuring their safe use seriously.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
articles.summary: Efforts to recover bodies after a “double-tap” attack in southern Ukraine are being hampered by continuing Russian strikes, officials say.

blocks.text: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images
ByMerlyn Thomas BBC Verify correspondent and Paul BrownBBC Verify
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there have been multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged.
"Due to the threat of repeated shelling, emergency workers are constantly forced to periodically suspend work and retreat to a safe place," it added.
The DSNS said the death toll had risen to at least 72 people making it one of the deadliest single incidents since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted

blocks.text: Image source, DSNS
Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted

Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.

blocks.caption: Emergency services workers leave a rubble filled area in Ukraine

blocks.text: Bodies are still to be recovered from the rubble, Oleksiy said. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead."
BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.

blocks.caption: Map of southern and eastern Ukraine showing areas under Russian military control and the location of Komyshuvakha, a village on the southern front line in Zaporizhzhia region. Russian-controlled territory is shaded pink, with limited Russian control shown by red hatching and claimed Russian contr…

blocks.text: A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.

While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.
Fears of second strike heard on police radios

Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.
Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in Ukraine
Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.
Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.

blocks.caption: Satellite image showing the site of the Komyshuvakha attack in Ukraine. White annotations highlight a large rectangular compound and surrounding buildings. A white dot marks the reported impact point inside the compound, while brackets indicate access points on the western side of the site. Two n…

blocks.text: The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.
Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.

Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.

blocks.caption: The crater was identified by experts as consistent with a 3,000kg bomb

blocks.text: Image source, Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.
His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The remnants of the wing from a glide bomb guidance kit

blocks.text: Image source, SBU
The remnants of the wing from a glide bomb guidance kit

Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.
International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.

Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".

Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.
Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

articles.title: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.summary: The reported strikes come a day after Ukraine launched its largest recorded drone attack on Russia since the start of the war, according to Moscow.

blocks.text: Two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital have reportedly been struck in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The missiles hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges spanning the Dnipro River, Klitschko said, adding that water and power supplies had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, Ukraine struck the landmark Kerch Bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea killing two people, the region's Moscow-installed governor said.

President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier warned that Moscow might launch further strikes on the country on Monday night, after Ukrainian, US and European officials held further talks aimed at ending the years-long conflict.
Those online talks, attended by US envoy Jared Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, came after Russia said it recorded the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems".
"Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services have been damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv. An estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
Separately, the Ukrainian military struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second consecutive day, the region's Moscow-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said on Telegram.
Traffic across the bridge had been suspended, he added.
The landmark bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014.

Russian President Vladimir Putin inaugurated the bridge to great fanfare in 2018. The severity of the latest strike on Kerch Bridge is still unclear, though it is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.

Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.
He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".
In an address on Monday evening, Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes.

Zelensky said that Europe was represented for the first time by the full delegation that will participate in negotiations with Moscow - including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the EU and Nato.
The Ukrainian president has long called for European delegates to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
He also said that Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.
Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.

Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title: Woman whose baby died after free birth didn’t know she was pregnant with twins, NSW inquest hears
articles.summary:
Inquest continues into deaths of four babies born in free births or home births in northern rivers

  • Get our

blocks.text: A northern rivers mother whose baby died after a free birth did not know she was having twins until she was in labour after having no pregnancy scans, the New South Wales coroner’s court has heard.

The inquest will examine the deaths of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. It will consider whether the care was reasonable in the circumstances and whether care by an unregistered support worker was reasonable and appropriate before, during and after the birth. Free births are when a person gives birth without a registered health professional present.

Both of the twins died – one was stillborn and most likely died in the womb before he was born, and one died after the birth, the inquest heard. Only Baby D, who was born alive, is included in the inquest – coroner’s courts can not examine the death of a stillborn baby.
The inquest heard on Tuesday that the mother – who cannot be named for legal reasons – had decided to do a “sovereign birth”, where a woman gives birth at home on her own.

The mother had three to four sessions with Sita Tara Kali, a self-described birth keeper, before the birth, according to a statement the mother gave to police that was read to the inquest. She was paid a fee of $4,100, the inquest heard.
Kali, who is expected to give evidence at a later date, was involved in the care of two of the four babies included in the inquest. She is not facing criminal charges.”

The mother said in the police statement that her sessions with Kali before the birth were “mostly bodywork”. She said: “I didn’t get anything much out of the system in terms of birth preparation, a few books. Nothing of the quality she offered me.”

blocks.caption: Self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali, also known as Mumma Sita. Photograph: gofundme.com

blocks.text: She said she felt “vibrant” and “healthy” during the pregnancy and the birth was “amazing”.
The mother only realised she was having another baby after giving birth to the first baby.
She said Kali advised them to ring an ambulance immediately, according to the police statement.
Sgt David Greenway told the inquest on Tuesday that when he arrived at the family’s house in 2024, he found one of the newborn twins had died. The other baby was on its way to hospital, he said.
The second twin, referred to as Baby D, did not survive.
Greenway said the parents were in shock and had not known they were expecting twins.
after newsletter promotion
Greenway told the inquest that Kali was present at the house and said to him: “I’m the birth keeper, so I support women that want to free birth.”

“I am not medically trained. And there is a big need because a lot of women don’t want to go to the hospital, and they can’t afford midwives. I’m not doing anything illegal. I know my rights,” Greenway recalled her saying.
“When people are choosing to be in their sovereignty, it is up to them what they choose to do,” Kali said, according to Greenway.

Dr Alison Teate, the president of the Australian College of Midwives, told the inquest on Tuesday if there are two twins and one placenta, they are at a higher risk category than if there are two placentas.
“The level of surveillance goes up significantly. It would be appointments every fortnight, from 20 weeks,” she said.

“Our decision to not systemize our birth was very prominent. We decided to not have scans and try to birth as holistically and spiritually as possible. Which would mean that we would have a home birth out of the system with a doula who is incredibly experienced.”
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Asylum seekers on final ‘one in, one out’ UK-France flight feel they are being ‘punished’
articles.summary:
Many of those onboard are being deported for second time after fleeing threats from people smugglers in France

Many of the asylum seekers on Tuesday’s final “one in, one out” deportation…

blocks.text: Many of the asylum seekers on Tuesday’s final “one in, one out” deportation flight are people who returned to the UK fleeing threats from smugglers after they were already forcibly returned to France.
Hundreds of asylum seekers who were sent back to France are thought to have returned to the UK, citing threats from smugglers who said their families still owed them money for the Channel crossing.

Asylum seekers who spoke to the Guardian described being punched, beaten or raped by the smugglers. Some said smugglers had caught them while they slept on the streets and forced them to work for them in conditions of modern slavery in a migrant camp in Calais, cleaning the smugglers’ tents and carrying water or firewood.
The charity Medical Justice, which has provided support to people detained for one in, one out, called the pilot scheme “a disaster”.

The one in, one out scheme involved forcibly returning hundreds of people who had travelled to the UK on small boats to France in exchange for bringing a similar number from northern France to the UK to claim asylum.

blocks.caption: Asylum seekers who were forcibly sent back to France said they had been threatened by smugglers who said they still owed them money for the Channel crossing. Photograph: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/Getty Images

blocks.text: One asylum seeker with a ticket for Tuesday’s flight said he was captured by the smugglers after being returned to France by the Home Office earlier this year. He said he was a political dissident in Iran, and believed he would be executed if he was returned there.
“I came back to the UK a second time because the smugglers caught me in France,” he said. “I was sleeping on the streets in Paris because France did not accept my asylum case.

“Many of the people who have tickets for Tuesday’s flight are people like me, who came back to the UK a second time. I believe those of us who came back to the UK a second time are being punished by being sent back to France a second time. I believe that 100%.”
He said that although the Home Office stated that sufficient lawyers were available for asylum seekers detained for France, he and others had struggled to access good quality legal advice.

“Friends paid privately for a lawyer for me. The lawyer promised me that 24 hours before the flight, they would challenge my removal, but he has done nothing,” he said. “They do not even answer the phone although I have tried to call them 10 times.
“My mind is broken. I am scared that when I am returned to France on Tuesday, the smugglers will catch me and kill me.

“When the guards came to take me to the plane for France last time, three or four of them surrounded me and made me feel like a criminal. I have committed no crime apart from coming to UK to claim asylum.
“When I slept on the street last time the weather was warmer in France. Now it is too cold to sleep outside. I don’t know what I’m going to do.”
after newsletter promotion
A second asylum seeker with a ticket for the flight, who also returned to the UK after being sent back to France, said he knew of dozens of people due to fly on Tuesday.
“All of us have bad solicitors who are not helping us,” he said. “One in, one out finished on 1 October. I do not understand why the Home Office wants to continue sending us to France.”

blocks.caption: One person who said he would be deported back to France on the last one in, one out flight said he feared being captured by smugglers who he had fled from. Photograph: Kiran Ridley/Getty Images

blocks.text: John Tuckett, the independent chief inspector of borders and immigration, said in a report published last week that it was not known how the Home Office would measure the success or failure of the one in, one out scheme, despite it being given the highest operational priority, with regular updates supplied to ministers and 10 Downing Street.

He cited a ministerial submission which stated that the aim of the scheme was to demonstrate that dangerous journeys on small boats were not a viable option for entry into the UK, with the aim of undermining the organised immigration crime model. Since the scheme ended on 1 October, 4,786 people have crossed the Channel in 69 small boats, according to government data.
A Medical Justice spokesperson said: “One in, one out has been a disaster, causing avoidable suffering to a vulnerable group and it has failed in the Home Office’s stated objective.
“The Home Office must start to learn lessons and put an end to dangerous detention conditions.”

Seema Syeda, of the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants, said: “The UK government has forced people fleeing war, climate breakdown and persecution to take murderous and traumatising journeys across the Channel, only to treat them with brutality once they have arrived here, retraumatising them with detention and deportation.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We welcome the inspector’s recognition of the strong operational delivery of the UK-France pilot, which successfully demonstrated that a returns arrangement of this kind can work.
“The message was clear: if you returned to the UK after being transferred to France under the pilot, you would be sent back.

“The pilot has now concluded and we are taking forward lessons learned as part of wider efforts to strengthen returns. Any future operational decisions, including on evaluation and reporting, will be considered in the usual way.”

articles.title: Serbia’s Student List candidates to be sworn in as MPs after election triumph
articles.summary:
Inaugural parliamentary session comes as ousted populist Aleksandar Vučić threatens mass protests of his own

Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political…

blocks.text: Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, are to be sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government.

The 140 candidates – among them academics, lawyers, scientists and the odd actor – will be sworn in on Tuesday during the inaugural session of the new parliament, bringing 14 years of rule by Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) to an end.

A caretaker government under the outgoing prime minister, Ðjuro Macut, will remain in office until MPs approve the Student List’s choice of a cabinet. For now, its makeup – including the identity of a future prime minister – remains unclear.

Sarah El Sarag, a human rights lawyer and MP-elect, said the wider student movement continued to be active in the process of selecting the cabinet, along with the candidates themselves. “We are there because of them,” she said of the students. “All the time, we are doing it together.”

blocks.caption: Student List supporters celebrate after Aleksandar Vučić concedes defeat in Serbia’s parliamentary election on 26 October. Photograph: Uros Arsic/Reuters

blocks.text: Parliamentary planning sessions had helped prepare the candidates, she said. “We have been having meetings and exercises for the parliament almost every day, because none of us are professional politicians. We are lawyers, doctors, professors – and it is the first time for us to do this kind of job.”

The sessions reflect the Student List’s efforts to pre-empt sceptics who question whether a group of candidates with no political experience is equipped to govern. Members of the movement that selected El Sarag and her fellow MPs-elect have reiterated that all are experts in their professional or academic fields and are better qualified than many of the people who served as ministers or MPs under Vučić.

El Sarag said her colleagues had a good idea of what to expect from Tuesday’s opening session. “People who have had some experience of politics have been making some simulated exercises for us,” she said.
She would not divulge the identity of the candidate for speaker – who will become Serbia’s acting president – let alone the name of the next prime minister.
after newsletter promotion

Vučić is not accepting his new role as leader of the opposition meekly. Since the election, he has accused the Student List of instituting a regime of “naked terror” by directing “submissive prosecutors and police” to carry out unlawful detentions.

Police and prosecutors have made a series of arrests of people with links to the SNS. Last week, prosecutors targeted the owners of a well-connected construction company over a project on the site of the once-famous Hotel Jugoslavija, which was hit during the 1999 Nato airstrikes on Belgrade.

That followed the arrest of the owner of Alta Bank, which held the concession for processing bill payments on behalf of Serbia’s state-owned electricity company. Others facing charges include senior police officers accused of abuse of office, and people suspected of vote rigging and violence during the elections.
After the two years of protests which culminated in the SNS’s defeat at the ballot box, Vučić is threatening major protests of his own.
Raša Nedeljkov, the programme director of the Serbian election and democracy monitor CRTA, said the first disruptions could come during parliament’s inaugural session.

“We can expect a lot of sabotage, a lot of obstruction, a lot of circus-creating atmosphere,” he said. “If we see such scenes in parliament – including some kind of physical obstruction – that’s something which would not surprise me.”

In such an atmosphere, speed may be of the essence, he said. MPs must approve a new cabinet within 90 days of the national assembly’s inaugural session but will be motivated to name a PM well before that deadline.

articles.title: Duterte camp urged to file report over alleged coercion of ex-staffer
articles.summary: This was after a post by lawyer Paolo Panelo, one of the legal counsels of the Vice President, saying that the Vice President received a message from what appeared to be the account of a former…

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 12:40pm
NBI director Melvin Matibag
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag urged the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte to file reports over alleged coercion of her former staff to sign a document.

This was after a post by lawyer Paolo Panelo, one of the legal counsels of the Vice President, noted that the vice president received a message from what appeared to be the account of a former household staff member containing a "desperate plea for help and rescue in Manila."
“They have to file a formal report. If they feel the urgency, dapat go through (the) legal process,” Matibag said in a message to Philstar.com.

According to Panelo, the sender claimed to be under the custody or control of certain individuals who allegedly warned of a threat to the former staffer's life and tried to force them to sign a document, which they refused to execute.
Panelo added that the individual's whereabouts and safety remain unverified.

Duterte’s lawyer also drew parallels between the alleged incident and that of Jefry Tupas, claiming that NBI agents had previously told Tupas on Sept. 29, 2026, of threats to his life before attempting to bring him to Manila.

“We are deeply concerned that this incident may be part of what we believe to be a relentless campaign by the Marcos administration, utilizing state institutions like the NBI, against the vice president,” Panelo said.

In a separate Facebook post, the vice president’s brother, Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City 1st District), condemned the alleged actions as a tactic to intimidate and pressure individuals into signing documents and acting as witnesses to fabricate a case against the Vice President.

“If your case is strong, then prove it in court. Stop intimidating people. Do not force anyone to become a witness through intimidation, coercion, or threats,” the vice president’s brother said in a Facebook post.

Aside from the impeachment trial, Duterte is also facing a grave threat charge before a Quezon City Regional Trial Court over her threats in October and November 2024 press conferences against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.

The NBI is also investigating alleged irregularities in the properties of the vice president and her husband, Manases Carpio, which are indicated in their Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth.

articles.title: Bishop laments ASEAN protest arrests on World Day of the Poor
articles.summary: "Poverty is not a crime," a bishop says, noting the irony of arrests of those raising concerns about communities and livelihoods.

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 11:56am

Protesters clash with police officers during a demonstration that coincides with the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Leaders' Summit and Related Summits in Manila on Nov. 15, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The Catholic Church was observing the World Day of the Poor when hundreds of Filipinos were arrested during the ASEAN summit protests on Sunday, November 15, San Carlos Bishop Gerardo Alminaza said.

The bishop pointed to the irony on Tuesday, saying the arrests came as protesters were raising concerns about their rights, livelihoods and communities, underscoring the need to protect the voices of marginalized Filipinos.

"Poverty is not a crime. Peaceful protest is not a crime. Demanding justice is not a crime," Alminaza said in a statement Tuesday, November 17. "The poor deserve a seat at the table and a meaningful voice in decisions that shape their future."
More than 300 people were reportedly arrested during demonstrations across Metro Manila as Southeast Asian leaders gathered for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

Alminaza urged the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) and other independent bodies to investigate reports of police abuse during the November 15 protests, including incidents involving journalists and a reported arrest on church property.
He also called on authorities to preserve evidence, allow independent access to detainees and hold personnel accountable for any violations.

"Authorities have a responsibility to protect public safety. That responsibility must be exercised with restraint and respect for human dignity. Allegations against particular individuals must be examined fairly; they must never become a blanket justification for punishing peaceful dissent," Alminaza said.
The bishop demanded the immediate release of those detained solely for exercising their right to peaceful assembly and the withdrawal of charges based only on such activities.

"I call for the immediate release of all those detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights, and for the withdrawal of charges based solely on such exercise. Every person in custody must have prompt access to legal counsel, family members and necessary medical care. Children must receive appropriate care, protection and assistance, with their best interests given priority," he said.

The Philippine National Police has defended its handling of the demonstrations, saying officers exercised maximum tolerance and that arrests were made in response to alleged obstruction of public roads and refusals to comply with authorities.

articles.title: Japan scrambles jets to counter suspected Russian aircraft
articles.summary: Japan said it lodged a "very stern protest" with Moscow after two suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace.

image.caption: Japan deployed jets to warn 'suspected Russian' aircraft that entered its airspace [Representative photo from September 2025]Image: Kurt Fairhurst/News Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Japan scrambled fighter jets in its airspace after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its territory on Tuesday morning, an incident that could further strain ties between the two countries.
Tokyo said it had lodged a "very stern protest" with Moscow after the incident.
Japan lodges protest against Russia over alleged airspace violation
The aircraft entered Japan's airspace near Okinoshima in southwestern Japan shortly after 4:00 a.m. local time Tuesday (1900 GMT Monday), Japanese ​Chief Cabinet ‌Secretary Minoru Kihara ‌said.

"The violation of our national airspace by Russian aircraft is not only a grave infringement of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our security and is completely unacceptable," Kihara said.
"We lodged a very stern protest with Russia through diplomatic channels and strongly demanded measures to prevent any recurrence," he said.
Japan had lodged a similar protest with Russia in 2024 after a Russian patrol plane entered its airspace three times, marking the first confirmed incursion since 2019.
Kihara said the aircraft travelled through the Tsushima Strait and went between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan before heading to the Pacific.
Strains increasing in Japan-Russia ties
Japan's relations with Moscow have soured over the past weeks after a Japanese journalist was arrested on spying allegations and after Russia seized four of Japan Tobacco's Russian assets.
Russia and Japan share a decades-old dispute over the status of a number of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
However, relations especially deteriorated further after Tokyo joined global sanctions against Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
South Korea says Russian aircraft entered defense zone

Tuesday's reported violation comes soon after South Korea said it too had deployed fighter jets and conducted tactical maneuvers after several Russian military aircraft entered its air defense zone in the early hours of Tuesday.
An air defense zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area in which countries identify approaching aircraft for security purposes.
Military aircraft are generally expected to notify the relevant country before entering its air defense zone, though this is not legally required.

articles.title: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
articles.summary: Votes are still being counted in the Alaska Senate race, with Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan.
articles.byline: Jake Horton, Thomas Copeland and Wesley Stephenson

blocks.text: ByJake Horton, Thomas Copeland and Wesley Stephenson
BBC Verify

Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.
This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".
US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.
But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

blocks.caption: A bar chart showing first-choice votes for each candidate: Mary Peltola (Dem): 141,637 votes, Dan S Sullivan (Rep): 130,162 votes, Gerald L Heikes (Rep): 6,020 votes, Daniel J Sullivan Jr: 4,684 votes, Write-in: 874 votes. After 98% of the votes counted.

blocks.text: Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.
BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.
The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.
This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.

items: Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state

blocks.caption: A bar chart showing the second choices of people who voted for Dan J Sullivan Jr, after 98% of votes counted. No valid second vote: 38%, Mary Peltola (Dem): 29%, Gerald L Heikes (Rep): 17%, Dan S Sullivan (Re-): 15%, Write-in: 1%

blocks.text: How did two Dan Sullivans end up in the race?
Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.

blocks.caption: Composite image showing side-by-side campaign-style portrait photographs of two different people. The person on the left wears a light green button-up shirt and stands outdoors against a pale sky and blurred mountain backdrop. A label beneath the portrait reads “Dan S Sullivan”. The person on the…

blocks.text: A New York Times story, external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.
Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.
President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".
But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.
"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.

items: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot

blocks.caption: Image caption, Senator Sullivan was joined by President Trump at a campaign rally ahead of the vote

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Senator Sullivan was joined by President Trump at a campaign rally ahead of the vote
How does voting work in Alaska?
Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.

"There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.
On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:
- Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.
- Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent
There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A sample ballot for the US Senate election in Alaska

blocks.text: Image source, Alaska Division of Elections
A sample ballot for the US Senate election in Alaska
As of Tuesday, Peltola holds 49.98% of the vote.

In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Democrat Mary Peltola's said on Saturday she will "decisively be elected" as Alaska's next senator

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Democrat Mary Peltola's said on Saturday she will "decisively be elected" as Alaska's next senator
What does ranked-choice voting data show so far?
Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".
Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.
We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.
A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.

"The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."
Additional reporting by Daniel Wainwright

articles.title: Rio Tinto agrees to pay US$250m to begin repairing ‘devastation’ left by Panguna mine
articles.summary:
Bougainville cabinet minister says fund gives chance to find solutions to ‘huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation’

Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has…

blocks.text: Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.

Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.
But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.

Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.
Theonila Roka Matbob, a Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.

“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.

“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”

blocks.caption: Bougainville minister Theonila Roka Matbob in her village of Mako ’Osi below the Panguna mine. Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian

blocks.text: Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”

The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.

“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”

The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.
Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.
“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.
“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”

Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.
“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”
The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.
The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.

The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.
What caused the Bougainville civil war?
Bougainville, a group of islands off Papua New Guinea to the north of Australia, has been variously controlled by Britain, Germany, Japan, Australia and PNG.
It declared independence in 1975 as the Republic of North Solomons, but was absorbed into the newly independent PNG weeks later.
Its close ethnic ties and proximity to the Solomons archipelago means it has always sat uneasily with Port Moresby’s rule.
That discontent came to a violent head in 1988 after a long-running dispute over the lucrative Panguna copper and gold mine.
The mine, carved from a mountain in central Bougainville, was critically important to PNG, at one point generating more than 45% of the country's national export revenue.

Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly US$2bn from the mine over 17 years of operation. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands had been destroyed by it.
Under the leadership of a former mine worker, Francis Ona, disaffected Bougainvilleans ran a sabotage campaign which forced the mine’s closure in 1989.

The PNG Government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war that ran for a decade, and saw as many as 20,000 people die.
PNG later hired international mercenaries to end the conflict (the notorious Sandline affair), before a peace agreement was signed in 2001.
In a 2019 referendum, 97.7% of Bougainvilleans voted in favour of independence. Many argue that reopening Panguna mine will be key to the island’s economic future as an independent nation.

Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.

Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.

A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.

The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.
The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.

But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.

articles.title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
articles.summary: Pakistan's ex-prime minister, who has been in prison since August 2023, says he has been denied justice.

blocks.text: Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.
"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.
Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.

Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.
Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".
He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.
"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.

He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.
He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year.
"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.
Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing".
"[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.
Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.
At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.
Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics.

Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

articles.title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
articles.summary: Sensor Tower estimates the game has already made $1.18bn from pre-orders across PlayStation and Xbox

blocks.text: Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.

When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding, external more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.
Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing , externaltaking several days off to play.
GTA 6 is no exception, but it appears to characteristically be taking things to a whole new level.
For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.
It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.

According to the HR firm, one person put "new GTA is coming out! I will be spending a week on the sofa in my pants!" as the reason for their leave request, while another said: "play the new GTA - I've waited a billion years".
A third said in their request: "GTA Release - I'll put my notice in if this is denied."
The company added it had no way of tracking if the requests had actually been approved by employers.
Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.

Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.
This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.
According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.
Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.
"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.
"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.
It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.

But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.
GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither has Sony nor Microsoft.

Louise Wooldridge from analyst firm Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".
Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.
Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.
"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.
A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.
Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.
Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.
"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.
"The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."
After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter what the cost or extra effort.

articles.title: Volunteers back in Manitoba after grounding of U.S. flights set them on long road trip home
articles.summary: A group of Manitobans doing volunteer work are back home after Friday's closure of U.S. airspace forced them on a long journey across that country.

image.caption: Doug Brown, a former Winnipeg Blue Bombers player working for a health-care equipment company, was among a group of about 40 people who took a 28-hour bus trip on their way back from a volunteer journey to Central America. (Submitted by Doug Brown)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New
A group of Manitobans doing volunteer work are back home after Friday's closure of U.S. airspace forced them on a long journey across that country.
28-hour bus trip anything but comfortable for about 40 returning from Nicaragua, including former Blue Bomber
Doug Brown was returning from Nicaragua with about 40 other volunteers with Operation Walk Manitoba, a charity that provides surgical treatments to people in developing countries.

The former Winnipeg Blue Bombers player works for a medical device company. He was aboard a flight from Managua to Houston, Texas, when he learned U.S. authorities had grounded flights nationwide, causing tens of thousands of flight cancellations over the weekend.
"We were literally just about an hour and a half out of Houston, and we all found out via the internet," Brown said Monday.
"I thought it was some sort of AI-fabricated joke."
The nationwide stop, the longest in 25 years, was in place for about four hours Friday.
U.S. officials said a contractor was replacing a copper wire with fibre optic cable when an unknown issue triggered an air traffic control system outage.
Brown's plane landed in Houston, but the outage delayed a connecting flight that would take the cohort of volunteers he was with to Denver.

items: Winnipeg film producer, family resume trip to L.A. after 24-hour delay in Minneapolis
Winnipeg airport asks passengers to check flight status amid U.S. stoppage

blocks.text: With cancellations rolling over into Saturday morning, the charity chartered a bus driving the volunteers back to Winnipeg instead.
The trip was about 28 hours long, Brown said.
"First stop, we went to Walmart just so we could get supplies," he said.
He bought pillows, a blanket, electrolyte water and a couple of apples.
Two Americans would alternate driving the bus, one taking over while the other slept.
"We didn't stop for dinner. We didn't stop overnight. We just essentially stopped when the bus needed fuel," Brown said.
"When we finally got to Winnipeg…, I almost laid down on the ground," he said.
"We hadn't showered or whatever in 24 hours. I was able to brush my teeth twice, but [it was the] first time I've done that at truck stops, right?…. It was a different world."
Sense of perspective

A team of nearly 70 volunteers was in Nicaragua for more than a week as part of the mission, with medical professionals performing hip replacement surgery to patients with severe joint disease who can't access that kind of care in the Central American country.
Medical lead Eric Bohm was in a cohort that managed to avoid disruptions while getting back to Manitoba.
Eric Bohm welcomed the volunteers who were left stranded in Texas after the U.S. ground stop. (Submitted by Doug Brown)
Bohm said those who made it home as planned wanted to make the other volunteers feel special. He was there to receive them at the end of their trip in Winnipeg.
"I thought … these guys are going to be tired and hungry and a little bit bummed out," Bohm said.
"Let's try to welcome them back home with some posters and some people showing up and some gift bags.… Just remind them, you know, how much the people in Nicaragua appreciate what they're doing."

items: Canada-wide flight grounding unlikely, says aviation expert

blocks.text: Brown said he used to take a bus with the Bombers to Regina for the Labour Day Classic, but those trips were only about a quarter of the length of the 28-hour journey over the weekend.
He said nobody wanted anyone else to be in charge of the music. Everyone also wanted to avoid using the one tiny bathroom that was available.
At six feet eight inches tall, sitting in the bus was uncomfortable enough for the former professional athlete.
But Brown said the trip to Nicaragua gave him a sense of perspective.
"One of the surgeons on the bus ride said, you know, Nicaragua was one of the poorest nations in the entire Western Hemisphere.…
"This is still nothing compared to what the vast majority of those people go through on a daily basis."
Senior officials in U.S. President Donald Trump's administration blamed the grounding on aging air traffic control infrastructure and Congress underfunding.
With files from Meaghan Ketcheson
