articles.title: Gordie Howe bridge surpasses 1M vehicle crossings while other bridges, tunnel lose traffic
articles.summary: The Gordie Howe International Bridge has seen more than a million crossings since it officially opened to vehicle traffic on July 27, according to new numbers from the Bridge and Tunnel Operators…

image.caption: The Gordie Howe International Bridge had seen 1,051,470 crossings as of Oct. 31. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor

The Gordie Howe International Bridge has seen more than a million crossings since it officially opened to vehicle traffic on July 27, according to new numbers from the Bridge and Tunnel Operators Association.
Windsor-Detroit tunnel remains the most popular passenger vehicle crossing, CEO says
Meanwhile, vehicle traffic over the Ambassador and Blue Water bridges and through the Windsor-Detroit Tunnel has declined.
The numbers cover the first three full months since the Gordie Howe opened.
They show the bridge averaging around 248,000 passenger vehicle crossings per month and slightly fewer than 85,000 truck crossings.
In a statement, the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority said, too, that more than 48,000 pedestrians and cyclists had used the bridge's multi-use path.

"The Gordie Howe International Bridge supports the efficient and effective movement of traffic in the Windsor-Detroit gateway by providing additional capacity, crossing choice and highway-to-highway connectivity for travellers and commercial operators crossing the border," the statement read.
"We are encouraged by the continued interest in the bridge and the growth in traffic volumes as more users become familiar with the crossing."
Windsor-Detroit Tunnel crossings were down just shy of 19 per cent between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31, while crossings at the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia were down approximately 12.5 per cent.
The Ambassador Bridge saw the biggest decline in total crossings — down nearly 32 per cent compared with the same period last year.
Tunnel CEO not surprised by numbers
Most of that decline was in passenger vehicle traffic, not truck traffic.

Truck crossings were off just 8.75 per cent since the same August-through-October period last year, despite hopes among some residents of Sandwich Town that the new bridge would ease traffic congestion on Huron Church Road.
Truck crossings at the Blue Water Bridge were down just over 30 per cent.
Windsor-Detroit Tunnel CEO Tal Czudner said he’s not surprised by the numbers.
Tunnel CEO Tal Czudner said he is happy to see the tunnel, which is jointly owned by the cities of Windsor and Detroit, remain the most popular passenger vehicle crossing. (CBC)

“[The Ambassador Bridge] had a very long runway to negotiate some very favorable deals with different … trucking companies. And obviously they own a decent amount of trucking infrastructure themselves.”

Truck crossings at the Ambassador Bridge remain up 3.85 per cent for the period running from Jan. 1 to the end of October, compared with the same period last year, while overall bridge traffic is down 6.82 per cent over the same time period.
Czudner said he is happy to see the tunnel, which is jointly owned by the cities of Windsor and Detroit, remain the most popular passenger vehicle crossing.
He also said the Windsor side of the operation has lost less traffic than the Detroit side.

“I think what you're finding is there's a lot of the people who work in automotive, manufacturing, healthcare, live in Windsor-Essex, take the tunnel to work, and then they take the Gordie Howe home,” he said.

“From a pricing perspective, that's actually the cheapest way to go. If you sign up for a [tunnel] Nexpress account, it’s the cheapest way to get from Windsor to Detroit. And if you sign up for a Breakaway account with Gordie Howe, that's the cheapest way to get from Detroit back to Windsor.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Heather Kitching reports local news for CBC stations across Ontario and the North. You can reach her at heather.kitching@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Exodus in Poilievre's office as 5 staffers plan departures
articles.summary: Sources tell CBC News five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit. The departures will leave big gaps in Poilievre's office,…

image.caption: The departures come as the Conservatives prepare for six byelections in December. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Sources tell CBC News five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit. The departures will leave big gaps in Poilievre's office, particularly in communications and policy.
Directors, senior-level staff informed Opposition leader of plans to leave: sources
Five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit, according to sources.
Those leaving their posts include the deputy chief of staff and director of policy, Aaron Wudrick, who informed caucus last week.
Others include director of communications and issues management, Micah Green, and director of media relations Sam Lilly.
Both are taking new jobs with the newly elected British Columbia Conservative government.
Senior policy adviser Andrew Evans and Poilievre's executive assistant Hayley Quipp have also informed the leader of plans to depart.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to share details about the internal workings of Poilievre's office, but Lilly and Green confirmed their departures in statements.
These departures will leave big gaps in the Opposition leader's office (OLO), particularly in communications and policy.

Wudrick is a longtime Conservative and respected by caucus, previously serving as director of domestic policy at the right-leaning Macdonald-Laurier Institute. Before that, he was the federal director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation.
He was one of the architects of the party's platform in the 2025 election campaign and has served in OLO for two-and-a-half years.

He was recently promoted to deputy chief of staff. His resignation follows other high-level departures from Poilievre's office earlier this year, including former chief of staff Ian Todd and former director of communications Katy Merrifield.
In an email sent to caucus last week, Wudrick said he would be leaving his role effective Nov. 27 for a job in the private sector in a bid to spend more time with his family.

"It has been an honour and a privilege to serve our leader and this team the last 2.5 years," he wrote, adding that he believes the goal of electing Poilievre to be prime minister "remains achievable in the next election."
Evans has been senior policy adviser since 2024, and previously held roles as a staffer in the Ford government. He was assigned to the immigration file, which has been a focus of the Opposition.
Green and Lilly are Poilievre's office's most senior communications staff. Green replaced Merrifield in April, but has been at OLO in a communications role since December 2022.
His LinkedIn page says he's been working for the Conservatives, either at OLO, the party or through an MP's office, since 2019.

Lilly is a longtime figure on Parliament Hill. He's been in communications with OLO since April 2021, starting as a press secretary and rising to director of media relations. In the 2019 election, he was a candidate for the Conservatives in Edmonton Strathcona.
These departures come as Poilievre faces pressure to keep seats in upcoming byelections after losing nine MPs since the 2025 election.

So far, he has lost four MPs to floor-crossing and four others have either announced plans to resign or have already resigned. Another MP, Quebec's Richard Martel, was appointed to the Senate. He still serves in the Conservative caucus.

items: Carney calls December byelections for 6 ridings in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan

blocks.text: There are six byelections in December.. The Conservatives are incumbents in two: Ontario's Brantford-Brant South and Saskatchewan's Yorkton-Melville.

Both seats were previously considered safe for the Conservatives, but the Carney Liberals' high polling in Ontario could see a fight in Brantford-Brant South, which was vacated by former justice critic Larry Brock.
Brock endorsed a local pastor, Dave Carrol, to succeed him — but the party chose Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis. Carrol later chose to run as an Independent, which risks splitting the Conservative vote.

items: Conservatives criticized over appointment of Brantford, Ont., Mayor Kevin Davis to run in byelection

blocks.text: Online posts and local news reports show Poilievre has been spending time in the riding, including this weekend, in a bid to shore up support.
Conservative sources who have spoken to CBC News in the past say, despite challenging polls, there is no plan to try to remove Poilievre and that he has the support of caucus.
Poilievre sailed through his last leadership review in January with 87.4 per cent of the vote from party members.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
articles.summary: Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

image.caption: Philippe Diallo is the third candidate for FIFA's presidency.Image: Bruno Bebert/Bestimage/IMAGO

blocks.text: French federation chief Philippe Diallo was "unanimously" backed by UEFA to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chiefGianni Infantino growing.
European football's governing body said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, with UEFA's "full support" behind the Frenchman.
Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.
Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support of five of FIFA's 211 member associations, before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

blocks.caption: Gianni Infantino seeks another term as FIFA presidentImage: Harry Langer/DeFodi Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Son of boxer, head of French football
Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the French Football Federation (FFF), is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.
He was appointed as FFF president in 2023 after being elected with a large majority. He was reelected in 2024 for another four-year term.
Back in September, Diallo said the FFF withdrew its support of Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying the trust in the FIFA President "has been betrayed."
"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said about the decision.
The Frenchman could become FIFA's first black president, while also being the organization's third head from France, after first president Robert Guerin and third president Jules Rimet.

blocks.caption: FIFA will hold the vote for its next president in MarchImage: Ennio Leanza/EPA/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Embattled Infantino
Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.
He has been facing growing criticism since his plan of selling parts of the World Cup to private investors. The criticisms were led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan, but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US trying to gather evidence, ahead of potentially complaining to Swiss authorities about alleged "criminal mismanagement" by Infantino.
FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.
Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round of 16 game against Belgium despite being shown a red card in the previous game.
The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.
FIFA wanted a World Cup without politics — it got Trump

articles.title: EU sanctions Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, Russia's richest woman
articles.summary: Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, has been the target of Ukrainian attacks for its role in supplying the Russian military. The EU has now frozen its owner's assets and banned her from…

image.caption: Both Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim and the Kremlin deny the company is involved in Russia's war in Ukraine, Kyiv sees things very differentlyImage: Sergei Fadeichev/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Union added Russia's wealthiest woman, online retailer Wildberries' CEO and owner Tatyana Kim, to its Russian sanctions list on Monday.
Kim's EU assets will be frozen as a result and she is barred from making financial transactions in or traveling to the bloc.
Kim, born in Grozny, Chechnya, to ethnic Korean parents, has an estimated net worth of $8.1 billion (€7.4 billion).
The sanctions were part of a larger regime targeting some 50 banks and oil export enablers and nearly 100 business leaders, propagandists and a major pro-Russian hacking group.

EU authorities say they targeted ​Kim due to the fact that Wildberries is "one of the largest taxpayers" in Russia and "operates as a supply network ​for the Russian military by facilitating the sale of military and ​dual-use ‌goods."
An EU statement went on to say that "Kim is supporting, materially or financially, and benefiting from Russia's military and industrial complex."
Wildberries is Russia's largest e-commerce retailer.
Why is the EU targeting an online retailer?

In its defense against invading Russian forces, Ukraine expanded its military target list this summer to include Wildberries warehouses inside Russia, saying the company's product list — which includes night-vision goggles, ammunition pouches and helmets alongside ‌regular clothing, cosmetics and electronics — is supporting Russia's illegal war.
Kim defended her company at the time, saying its offerings were no different than other online retailers like Amazon in the US and Alibaba in China.
The Kremlin, too, denied that the company and its warehouses were involved in the war effort.
Why Ukraine is targeting Russia's biggest online retailer
Who else is on the EU's newest sanctions list?
In a statement, Wildberries said Brussels' sanctions would have no impact on the company since it has no assets in the bloc nor does it conduct business there.
Other entities on Monday's sanctions list include firms in China, Oman, the Seychelles and the United Arab Emirates linked to the sale of oil from Russia's so-called shadow fleet of illicit tankers.
The sale of that oil also fuels Russia's invasion, which the EU is seeking to hamper through sanctions as well as direct financial and military assistance for Kyiv.

Brussels has imposed more than 20 sanctions packages in response to Russia's February 24, 2022, invasion of Ukraine, targeting thousands of individuals and companies to pressure President Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the assault.
The 27-nation bloc intends to introduce another sweeping sanctions package by year's end.
Oil smuggling via Russia's shadow fleet raises concerns

articles.title: Pakistan: Former leader Khan pleads for medical care
articles.summary: Imran Khan appealed to judges to be treated "before it's too late." His wife was also included in the request.

image.caption: Imran Khan says the accusations against him are politically motivatedImage: PPI/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former PakistanPrime Minister Imran Khan appealed to the country's Supreme Court in a bid to receive urgent medical attention for himself and his wife.

According to an open letter conveyed to the court through Khan's lawyer, the former leader's doctors had warned him of a risk for brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest and that his blood pressure had risen sharply.
He also said his wife Bushra Bibi required further eye operation, and that she is at risk of losing her eyesight should she not be granted the surgery.
The letter was released to the public by Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar.
"Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” the letter reads, asking the judges to give him "justice" before it was too late.
"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," Khan wrote.
Government contests account
An earlier court order ordered Khan's transfer to a hospital in Pakistani capital Islamabad, with Khan alleging that the authorities had not implemented it.
However, cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said Khan was receiving medical care, while also receiving food and books of his liking.
According to Chaudhry, the former leader has been taken to medical examinations at a hospital in Islamabad eight times, with his health and blood pressure being found to be in order.
Still a popular figure

Despite being in prison since 2023 for corruption offenses, Khan is still considereda popular figure in Pakistan, with his party demanding his release. His wife is alo serving jail time for graft offenses.
Khan argues the charges against him are politically motivated, which the government denies.

The government, led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, also denied Khan was in solitary confinement. More than 900 visits to Khan have been registered since he started his jail time in 2023, according to the authorities.

blocks.caption: Imran Khan is still a popular figure in PakistanImage: PPI/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a previous case, Khan's attorney told the court that his client had lost about 85% of his right eye's vision. However, his sister later said his situation was improving.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia challenged by Yemeni allies over ceding ground to Houthis
articles.summary:
Strategy of redeploying forces to try to relieve siege of Taiz and protect Aden comes as Islamist group makes steady gains

Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.

The Saudi-backed government explained the repositioning by saying the strategic priority was to break the attritional siege on Taiz, Yemen’s third city, and to protect Aden, the southern port city in which the Saudi-backed and UN-recognised government is now based.

Many blame the Houthi advance on the absence of a consolidated military command and control among the disparate forces backing the Aden-based government. Saudi Arabia responded to the setback by sidelining the commander of its Yemen coalition, Lt Gen Fahd bin Abdulaziz al-Salman, and replacing him with the chief of staff, Gen Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad al-Ruwaili.

The Houthis’ steady advance towards the areas surrounding Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait linking the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean on Yemen’s west coast, culminated on Sunday with a formal withdrawal of Yemen government forces, including some in the Southern Giants Brigades that had always been reluctant to defend territory outside the old southern Yemen. In 1990 Yemen had been divided in two, and many in the south want to return to a separated state.
The Saudi-backed government launched a fresh military campaign 42 days ago to drive the Houthis from Yemen but so far it has backfired.
The forces redeployed on Sunday have moved along the coast to al-Suqyah, 95 miles west of Aden, and inside the old Southern Yemen.
The retreat seems to be acknowledgment of Houthi resilience and is all the more remarkable given the Saudi air superiority. More than 300,000 Yemeni civilians have been displaced.

Amr al-Bidh, special representative of the exiled Southern Transitional Council (STC) leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, a separatist anti-Houthi force that is opposed by Saudi Arabia, accused the Saudis of incompetence – and in effect warned Riyadh that unless it became more open to a southern state it would lack the cohesive forces required to prevent the Houthis becoming a permanent security threat.

He said: “When there is no strategy and no plan, it is inevitable the Saudis would take advantage. The STC will defend the south to the last man but we are fighting with one hand behind our backs since January after Saudi Arabia attacks on the STC.

“The STC forces retain a credible capability on the ground. But we need practical and political support from the region to counter the Houthis and create the basis for a negotiated settlement, one in which the pathway towards southern independence is fully recognised. We cannot continue like this or else the Houthis will keep expanding.”

The breadth of support for the STC, backed by the United Arab Emirates, however, remains disputed. The movement suffered a near fatal setback in January and since then some of the Giants Brigades have switched to backing Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia continues in effect to keep as many as 10 STC leaders hostage in Riyadh, and has refused to let al-Zubaidi to return from exile in Abu Dhabi. Al-Bidh argued the priority should be defensive, avoiding counteroffensives that backfire, improving command and control, and widening the coalition.

Al-Bidh said reconciliation would require Riyadh to acknowledge the political declaration al-Zubaidi made about a timetable for a southern state in January, and that al-Zubaidi’s return would boost morale and help unify chaotic southern military factions.

He said a recent Yemeni government cabinet reshuffle, including a new information minister, was designed primarily to try draw southerners into fighting the Houthis and not to change policy toward the south.

He also urged the UK to use its diplomacy to bring in other actors rather than simply backing Riyadh. A group of southern Yemenis have written to the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, seeking a review of UK policy. “We recognise that the longstanding advice from your office is to continue following the Saudi line while calling for unity among the anti-Houthi forces,” the letter said. “But you must surely recognise that every time Britain calls for ‘the unity and territorial integrity of Yemen’, it is asking the southern people and their armed forces to fight for a political outcome in which they do not believe”.

The former US special envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking said the US administration was treating Yemen like a sideshow adding “world powers do not understand the gravity of what it is at stake here”. He warned “the problem is only going to get bigger through apathy and lack of attention”.

articles.title: Grammy Awards: Raye and Rosalia lead nominations
articles.summary: The nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards are in and women dominated the top categories for the highest accolade in the music industry.

image.caption: Raye received 11 Grammy nominationsImage: Mike Gray/Avalon/IMAGO

blocks.text: British singer Raye, with the genre mixing hit "Where Is My Husband!," landed at the top of the list of Grammy Award nominees on Monday, followed by Spanish musician Rosalia and "Choosin" Texas" artist Ella ‌Langley.
Raye earned 11 ⁠Grammy ⁠nominations including nods for song and record of the year for "Husband," and for album of the year for "This Music May Contain Hope."
She now ties Beyonce's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.
For her part, Rosalia received nine nominations, just days after sweeping the Latin Grammys with ​her album "Lux."

blocks.caption: Rosalia mixes genres such as flamenco and popImage: Julie Sebadelha/AFP

blocks.text: First-time nominee Langley secured seven, as did Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers.
Megastar Taylor Swift received five nominations.
Only one male artist nominated for Best Album

Besides Raye, competitors in the album race include Taylor Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl," Langley's "Dandelion," Rosalia's "Lux," Bridgers' "Lost Weekend," Olivia Dean's "The Art of Loving," and Rodrigo's "you ​seem pretty sad for a girl so in love." Bruno Mars was the only male artist nominated in the category, for his album "The Romantic."

blocks.caption: Taylor Swift, has taken the album of the year trophy a record four timesImage: Caroline Brehman/REUTERS

blocks.text: The record of the year category is made up of Dean's “Man I Need,” Langley's “Choosin' Texas,” Mars' “I Just Might,” Raye's “Where Is My Husband!”, Rodrigo's “The Cure,” Rosalía’s “Berghain” featuring Björk and Yves Tumor, Swift's “The Fate of Ophelia” and Tame Impala and Jennie's “Dracula.”

K-pop sensation ⁠BTS declined to submit any ​music for consideration in protest over a new Asian pop music category. Members of the South Korean band said they did not believe music should be categorized by region.

blocks.caption: K-pop powerhouse BTS said in July they are not interested in winning a new Asian music categoryImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Dolly Parton, the country legend who died in August, received three posthumous nominations.
Winners will be announced on February
The final Grammy voting round will run from December 10 to January 7, with winners selected by around 16,000 Recording Academy members.
Winners will be announced at a red-carpet ceremony in downtown Los Angeles ‌on ​February 7.
The event will be broadcast live on Walt Disney's ABC and streamed on Disney+ and Hulu.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
articles.summary: When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into…

image.caption: Voyager 1: Destined to wander the Milky Way "eternally"Image: NASA/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.
Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.
NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.
But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.
Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.
It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.
How did Voyager 1 get so far and where is it going?
In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.
On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.
In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.
That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.
Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

blocks.caption: There were two Golden Records, one on Voyager 1 and another on Voyager 2, a second spacecraft on the same 1970s mission. They were protected with this gold aluminum cover.Image: United Archives/picture alliance

blocks.text: Voyager 1 is an ongoing scientific experiment
The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.
"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.
Something you didn't already know about Voyager 1
No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.
We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.
NASA launches new telescope to explore hidden universe

articles.title: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
articles.summary: In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson will be the new James BondImage: Amazon MGM Studios

blocks.text: After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.
This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.
The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history.
How it all started
The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.
Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

blocks.caption: Bond girls were typically portrayed as ditzy blondes with little to sayImage: IFTN/United Archives/IMAGO

blocks.text: A machismo problem
Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.
Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.
In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.
Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

blocks.caption: The first bond girl was named Honey Ryder, a name which would likely be considered sexist by today's standardsImage: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Questionable lifestyle choices

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

blocks.caption: Even such artwork associated with the original Bond film would never be deemed appropriate in this day and ageImage: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why are all secretaries women?
In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.
Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.
Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.
In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

blocks.caption: It wasn't until the 2012 film that we finally learn something about Bond's boss's secretary, MoneypennyImage: CAP/MFS Image/Capital Pictures/picture alliance

blocks.text: Inappropriate casting

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.
If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

blocks.caption: White actor Joseph Wiseman was made to look Asian with makeupImage: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pattinson as a modern 007?

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.
Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.
This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

articles.title: The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: how close are the connections?
articles.summary: The Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has become a focal point for the far right. Many of its members and staff have ties to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations.

image.caption: The new AfD youth wing 'Generation Germany' was set up in 2025Image: Marcus Golejewski/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, she has set herself an ambitious goal: together with her co-chair Alice Weidel, she aims to see Germany's next chancellor come from their party.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?
Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.
How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD?
The normalization of right-wing extremism?

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas."

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

Particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it."
The debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?

Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.
Young, far-right and radical? Meet the AfD's future leaders
Controversial distancing efforts within the AfD

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?"

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization."
Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.
* Editor's note: To protect the privacy of the staff member of Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts, we have changed her name to Laura Neumann. Her real name is known to the editors.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
articles.summary:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore…

blocks.text: Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

blocks.caption: Hope Hostel in Kigali was prepared to house asylum seekers sent from Britain to Rwanda under the Conservatives’ prepared scheme.  Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

blocks.caption: The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said the return hubs offered ‘a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe’.  Photograph: Radek Miča/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.
